### Foreign policy views

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=38 "Edit section: Foreign policy views")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/US_congressional_delegation_at_HISF_2014.jpg/250px-US_congressional_delegation_at_HISF_2014.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_congressional_delegation_at_HISF_2014.jpg)

US congressional delegation at [Halifax International Security Forum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax_International_Security_Forum "Halifax International Security Forum") 2014

Cotton, through his foreign policy views, has been characterized as a [war hawk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_hawk "War hawk").[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-:1-161)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-162)

During a February 5, 2015, [Senate Armed Services Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Armed_Services "United States Senate Committee on Armed Services") hearing, Cotton called for housing more prisoners at [Guantanamo Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guantanamo_Bay_detention_camp "Guantanamo Bay detention camp") instead of closing it. He said of the detainees in the camp, "every last one of them can rot in hell, but as long as they don't do that they can rot in Guantanamo Bay".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-trumpism-9)[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-163) The following June, he was one of 21 Senate Republicans to oppose an amendment to the 2016 Defense Authorization Act that would impair any future president's ability to authorize torture. The amendment, which passed, had bipartisan support and was sponsored by [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain "John McCain") and [Dianne Feinstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dianne_Feinstein "Dianne Feinstein").[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-164)[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-165)

In September 2016, Cotton was one of 34 senators to sign a letter to [United States secretary of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State")[John Kerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerry "John Kerry") advocating that the United States use "all available tools to dissuade Russia from continuing its airstrikes in Syria" from an [Iranian airbase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Iranian_Air_Force_bases "List of Iranian Air Force bases") near [Hamadan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamadan "Hamadan") "that are clearly not in our interest" and saying the US should clearly enforce the violation of "a legally binding Security Council Resolution" on Iran.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-166)

In July 2017, Cotton voted in favor of the [Countering America's Adversaries Through Sanctions Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countering_America's_Adversaries_Through_Sanctions_Act "Countering America's Adversaries Through Sanctions Act") that grouped together [sanctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_sanctions "International sanctions") against [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"), [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran") and [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea").[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-167)

In December 2018, after Trump announced the withdrawal of [American troops in Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American-led_intervention_in_the_Syrian_Civil_War "American-led intervention in the Syrian Civil War"), Cotton was one of six senators to sign a letter expressing concern about the move and their belief "that such action at this time is a premature and costly mistake that not only threatens the safety and security of the United States, but also emboldens ISIS, Bashar al Assad, Iran, and Russia."[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-168) In January 2019, Cotton was one of 11 Republican senators to vote to advance legislation intended to block Trump's intent to lift sanctions against three Russian companies.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-169)

In August 2019, it was reported that Cotton had suggested to Trump and the Danish ambassador that the U.S. should buy [Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland "Greenland").[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-170)[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-171)[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-172) Cotton supports U.S. withdrawal from the [Open Skies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_on_Open_Skies "Treaty on Open Skies") agreement, which lets nations use special aircraft to monitor each other's military activities. In 2018, he asserted that the agreement was outdated and that it favored Russian interests.[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-173)

#### China

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=39 "Edit section: China")]

In 2018, Cotton was a cosponsor of the Countering the Chinese Government and Communist Party's Political Influence Operations Act, a bill introduced by [Marco Rubio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Rubio "Marco Rubio") and [Catherine Cortez Masto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Cortez_Masto "Catherine Cortez Masto") that would grant the U.S. secretary of state and the director of national intelligence (DNI) the authority to create an interagency task force with the purpose of examining attempts by China to influence the U.S. and key allies.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-174)

In August 2018, Cotton and 16 other lawmakers urged the Trump administration to impose sanctions under the [Global Magnitsky Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnitsky_Act#Global_Magnitsky_Act "Magnitsky Act") against [Chinese officials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_China "Communist Party of China") who are responsible for [human rights violations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang_re-education_camps "Xinjiang re-education camps") in western [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")'s [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang") region targeting the [Uyghur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs") ethnic minority.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-175) They wrote in a bipartisan letter, "The detention of as many as a million or more Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim ethnic minorities in 'political reeducation' centers or camps requires a tough, targeted, and global response".[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-176)

In February 2019, Cotton was one of the group of Senate Republicans who signed a letter to [Speaker of the House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives "Speaker of the United States House of Representatives")[Nancy Pelosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi "Nancy Pelosi") requesting that Pelosi invite [President of Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Taiwan "President of Taiwan")[Tsai Ing-wen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsai_Ing-wen "Tsai Ing-wen") to address a joint meeting of Congress. The request came amid heightened tensions between the U.S. and China and was expected to anger Chinese leadership if granted.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-177)

In May 2019, when asked about the impact of tariffs on farmers in Arkansas, Cotton said there would be "some sacrifices on the part of Americans, I grant you that, but I also would say that sacrifice is pretty minimal compared to the sacrifices that our soldiers make overseas that are fallen heroes that are laid to rest in Arlington make", and that farmers were willing to make sacrifices in order for the U.S. to fend off Chinese attempts to displace the U.S. globally.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-178)

In May 2019, Cotton was a cosponsor of the South China Sea and East China Sea Sanctions Act, a bipartisan bill reintroduced by [Marco Rubio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Rubio "Marco Rubio") and [Ben Cardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Cardin "Ben Cardin") that was intended to disrupt China's consolidation or expansion of its claims of jurisdiction over both the sea and air space in disputed zones in the South China Sea.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-179)

In July 2019, Cotton and Senator [Chris Van Hollen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Van_Hollen "Chris Van Hollen") were the primary sponsors of the Defending America's 5G Future Act, a bill that would prevent Huawei from being removed from the "entity list" of the Commerce Department without an act of Congress and authorize Congress to block administration waivers for U.S. companies to do business with Huawei. The bill would also codify Trump's executive order from the previous May that empowered his administration to block foreign tech companies deemed a national security threat from conducting business in the United States.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-180)

In April 2020, Cotton said that Chinese students in the United States should be restricted to studying the humanities and banned from studying science-related fields. In an interview with Fox News, he said, "It is a scandal to me that we have trained so many of the Chinese Communist Party's brightest minds."[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-181)[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-182)

On August 10, 2020, the Chinese government [sanctioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_sanctions "Chinese sanctions") Cotton and 10 other Americans for "behaving badly on Hong Kong-related issues".[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-183)

In February 2021, Cotton released a report, "Beat China: Targeted Decoupling and the Economic Long War", that called for the U.S. to sever most economic ties with China and invest in scientific, technological, and manufacturing fields China is ahead in.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-:3-184) The report called for economic restrictions on China despite the costs, saying the "costs of targeted decoupling with China pale in comparison to the costs of passivity"; more sanctions against theft of U.S. intellectual property, controls on U.S. technologies exported to China; barring "Chinese nationals in graduate and post-graduate programs in the United States from studying or conducting research in sensitive science, technology, engineering, and mathematics fields"; and expanded trade relations with allied countries to mitigate the impact of decoupling with China. In a speech detailing the report, Cotton said, "We need to beat this evil empire and consign the Chinese Communists ... to the ash heap of history".[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-:3-184)

In March 2023, Cotton and Senator [Katie Britt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katie_Britt "Katie Britt") introduced the Not One More Inch or Acre Act, which would ban any Chinese national or Chinese entity from owning American land.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-185) Cotton and Britt introduced the bill again in January 2025.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-186)

In July 2023, Cotton criticized President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden")'s efforts to diplomatically engage with China, saying: "Biden administration officials should stop chasing after their Chinese communist counterparts like lovestruck teenagers. It's embarrassing and it's pathetic".[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-187)

In January 2024, Cotton questioned TikTok CEO [Shou Zi Chew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shou_Zi_Chew "Shou Zi Chew") during a Senate hearing on child safety on social media, repeatedly asking Shou whether he was a member of the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party"). Shou said he was not, as he was a citizen of [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore") and did not hold Chinese nationality. Cotton continued to question Shou about his nationality and politics. Shou continued to affirm his Singaporean nationality. Cotton received backlash, especially from [Singaporeans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singaporeans "Singaporeans"),[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-188)[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-189) for this incident.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-190)[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-191)

In February 2025, Cotton criticized [Elon Musk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elon_Musk "Elon Musk") for "chasing Chinese dollars" and having "shamefully supplicated China's Communist rulers" in his book, _Seven Things You Can't Say About China_.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-192)

#### COVID-19

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=40 "Edit section: COVID-19")]

On January 28, 2020, in the context of the emergence of [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), Cotton urged the Trump administration to halt commercial flights from China to the United States. On January 31, spurred in part by Cotton's warnings, the Trump administration banned most travel from China.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-193)[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-194)[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-195)[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-196)

In a February 16, 2020, Fox News interview,[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-197) Cotton said that the coronavirus may have started at the biosafety level 4 super laboratory in [Wuhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wuhan "Wuhan"), China. "Now, we don't have evidence that this disease originated there", Cotton said, "but because of China's duplicity and dishonesty from the beginning we need to at least ask the question".[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-NYT20200218-198)[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-WaPo20200217-199) Articles published by _The New York Times_ and _The Washington Post_ the same day reported that scientists had dismissed claims that the Chinese government created the virus. _The Times_ said this was because of its resemblance to the [SARS virus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severe_acute_respiratory_syndrome "Severe acute respiratory syndrome"), which originated with bats.[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-WaPo20200217-199)[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-NYT20200218-198) In another interview on Fox the next day, Cotton said of the two articles, "It tells you the Chinese Communist Party, just like any communist party, has a widespread propaganda effort."[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-200)_The Post_ called Cotton's comments "debunked" and "conspiracy theory" for 15 months until issuing a correction: "The term 'debunked' and _The Post_'s use of 'conspiracy theory' have been removed because, then as now, there was no determination about the origins of the virus." Molecular biologist [Richard Ebright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Ebright "Richard Ebright") said _The Post_ had omitted his views supporting the [lab leak hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lab_leak_theory "COVID-19 lab leak theory") and "materially misrepresented" his views, adding, "Watching 'the first rough draft of history' being written as a partisan exercise, rather than a journalistic exercise, was dismaying."[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-WaPo20200217-199)[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-201)

Cotton tweeted around March 2020: "we will hold accountable those who inflicted it on the world" for what it had done. To a tweet reading "China will pay for this", he responded, "Correct."[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-202) In late April 2020, Cotton said in a Fox News interview that the non-containment of the pandemic was a "deliberate" and "malevolent" attack by the Chinese government on the rest of the world. "They did not want to see their relative power and standing in the world decline because the virus was contained [in China]", he said.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-203)[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-204)

In early 2023, the [United States Department of Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy "United States Department of Energy") assessed that a "lab leak was to blame" for the emergence of COVID-19. The assessment, which mirrored a similar assessment by the FBI,[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-205) was made with a "low confidence" level. In response, Cotton said, "being proven right doesn’t matter. What matters is holding the Chinese Communist Party accountable so this doesn’t happen again."[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-206)[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-207)

#### Israeli–Palestinian conflict

**Thomas Bryant Cotton** (born May 13, 1977) is an American politician and former [Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army") officer serving since 2015 as the [junior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seniority_in_the_United_States_Senate "Seniority in the United States Senate")[United States senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") from [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"). From 2013 to 2015 he served in the [U.S. House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives"), representing [Arkansas's 4th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas's_4th_congressional_district "Arkansas's 4th congressional district"). He is a member of the [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)").

Cotton was elected to the House in [2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Arkansas#District_4 "2012 United States House of Representatives elections in Arkansas") and to the Senate in [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_United_States_Senate_election_in_Arkansas "2014 United States Senate election in Arkansas"), defeating incumbent [Mark Pryor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Pryor "Mark Pryor"). He is chair of the [Senate Republican Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_Republican_Conference "Senate Republican Conference") and the [Senate Intelligence Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Select_Committee_on_Intelligence "United States Senate Select Committee on Intelligence").

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Thomas Bryant Cotton was born on May 13, 1977, in [Dardanelle, Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dardanelle,_Arkansas "Dardanelle, Arkansas").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-1) His father, Thomas Leonard "Len" Cotton, was a district supervisor in the [Arkansas Department of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas_Department_of_Health "Arkansas Department of Health"), and his mother, Avis ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name") Bryant) Cotton, was a schoolteacher who later became principal of their district's middle school.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-2) Cotton's family had lived in rural Arkansas for seven generations, and he grew up on his family's cattle farm.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-superstar-4) He attended [Dardanelle High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dardanelle_High_School "Dardanelle High School"), where he played on the local and regional basketball teams; standing 6 ft 5 in (1.96 m) tall, he was usually required to play [center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_(basketball) "Center (basketball)").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-superstar-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-gitom-5)

Cotton was accepted to [Harvard College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_College "Harvard College") after graduating from high school in 1995. At Harvard, he majored in government and served on the editorial board of _[The Harvard Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Harvard\_Crimson "The Harvard Crimson")_, often dissenting from the liberal majority.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-gitom-5) In articles, Cotton addressed what he saw as "[sacred cows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacred_cow_(idiom) "Sacred cow (idiom)")" such as [affirmative action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affirmative_action "Affirmative action").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-6) He was a Claremont Institute Publius Fellow in 1997.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-7) He graduated with an [A.B.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts")_[magna cum laude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin\_honors#Distinctions "Latin honors")_ in 1998 after only three years of study. Cotton's senior thesis focused on _[The Federalist Papers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Federalist\_Papers "The Federalist Papers")_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-superstar-4)

After graduating from Harvard College in 1998, Cotton was accepted into a [master's program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master's_degree "Master's degree") at [Claremont Graduate University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claremont_Graduate_University "Claremont Graduate University"). He left in 1999, saying that he found academic life "too sedentary", and instead enrolled at [Harvard Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Law_School "Harvard Law School"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-superstar-4) graduating with his [Juris Doctor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor") in 2002.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-8)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

After graduating from Harvard Law School, Cotton spent one year as a [law clerk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_clerk "Law clerk") for Judge [Jerry Edwin Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Edwin_Smith "Jerry Edwin Smith") of the [U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Fifth_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit"). He then went into private practice as an associate at law firms [Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibson,_Dunn_&_Crutcher "Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher") and [Cooper & Kirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_J._Cooper#Cooper_&_Kirk "Charles J. Cooper") in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), until he commissioned in the U.S. Army in 2005.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-trumpism-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-Cooper&Kirk-10)

## Military service

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Military service")]

On January 11, 2005, Cotton [commissioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_service "Military service") in the [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-11) He entered [Officer Candidate School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officer_Candidate_School_(United_States_Army) "Officer Candidate School (United States Army)") (OCS) in March 2005 and was commissioned as a [second lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Lieutenant#United_States "Second Lieutenant") in June.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-DefensePAC-12) He completed [Ranger School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranger_School "Ranger School"),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-Salon-14) a 62-day small unit tactics and leadership program that earned him the [Ranger tab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabs_of_the_United_States_Army#Ranger "Tabs of the United States Army"), and [Airborne School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Airborne_School "United States Army Airborne School") to earn the [Parachutist Badge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parachutist_Badge_(United_States) "Parachutist Badge (United States)").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-DefensePAC-12)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Tom_Cotton_holding_a_kitten.jpg/250px-Tom_Cotton_holding_a_kitten.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tom_Cotton_holding_a_kitten.jpg)

Cotton in Baghdad, 2006

In May 2006, Cotton was deployed to [Baghdad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baghdad "Baghdad") as part of [Operation Iraqi Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Iraqi_Freedom "Operation Iraqi Freedom") (OIF) as a platoon leader with the [101st Airborne Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/101st_Airborne_Division "101st Airborne Division"). In [Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq "Iraq"), he led a 41-man [air assault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_assault "Air assault") infantry platoon in the [506th Infantry Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/506th_Infantry_Regiment "506th Infantry Regiment"), and planned and performed daily combat patrols.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-DefensePAC-12) In December 2006 Cotton was promoted to [first lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lieutenant#United_States "First Lieutenant") and reassigned to the [3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment (The Old Guard)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3rd_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States) "3rd Infantry Regiment (United States)") at [Fort Myer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Base_Myer%E2%80%93Henderson_Hall "Joint Base Myer–Henderson Hall") in Arlington, Virginia, as a platoon leader.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-15)

From October 2008 to July 2009, Cotton was deployed to eastern [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan "Afghanistan").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-16) He was assigned within the [Train Advise Assist Command – East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Train_Advise_Assist_Command_%E2%80%93_East "Train Advise Assist Command – East") at its Gamberi [forward operating base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward_operating_base "Forward operating base") (FOB) in [Laghman Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laghman_Province "Laghman Province") as the operations officer of a [Provincial Reconstruction Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provincial_Reconstruction_Team "Provincial Reconstruction Team") (PRT), where he planned daily [counter-insurgency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-insurgency "Counter-insurgency") and reconstruction operations.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-DefensePAC-12)

Cotton was honorably discharged in September 2009. During his time in the service, he completed two combat deployments overseas, was awarded a [Bronze Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Star_Medal "Bronze Star Medal"), two [Army Commendation Medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commendation_Medal "Commendation Medal"), a [Combat Infantryman Badge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat_Infantryman_Badge "Combat Infantryman Badge"), a [Ranger tab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabs_of_the_United_States_Army "Tabs of the United States Army"), an [Afghanistan Campaign Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan_Campaign_Medal "Afghanistan Campaign Medal"), and an [Iraq Campaign Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_Campaign_Medal "Iraq Campaign Medal").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-DefensePAC-12)

After his active-duty service, Cotton joined the management consulting firm [McKinsey & Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McKinsey_&_Company "McKinsey & Company").

In July 2010, Cotton entered the [Army Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Reserve "United States Army Reserve") (USAR). He was discharged in May 2013.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-MuckRock-17)

### 2006 letter to _The New York Times_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2006 letter to The New York Times")]

In June 2006, while stationed in Iraq, Cotton gained public attention after writing an open letter to the editor of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_, asserting three journalists had violated "espionage laws" by publishing an article detailing a [classified government program monitoring terrorists' finances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorist_Finance_Tracking_Program "Terrorist Finance Tracking Program"). The _Times_ did not publish Cotton's letter, but it was published on _[Power Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power\_Line "Power Line")_, a conservative blog that had been copied on the email.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-20) In the letter, Cotton called for the journalists to be prosecuted for [espionage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espionage "Espionage") "to the fullest extent of the law" and incarcerated. He accused the newspaper of having "gravely endangered the lives of my soldiers and all other soldiers and innocent Iraqis". Cotton's claims circulated online and were reprinted in full elsewhere.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-Bauman-21) According to [Jay Rosen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Rosen "Jay Rosen"), a professor of journalism at [New York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University "New York University") in 2011, the [Espionage Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espionage_Act_of_1917 "Espionage Act of 1917") has never been used against journalists. Rosen argued that accusing investigative journalists of engaging in espionage is "essentially saying that they're working for another power, or aiding the enemy. That is culture war tactics taken to an extreme."[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-Bauman-21)

### Army Ranger controversy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Army Ranger controversy")]

In 2021, [Salon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salon_(website) "Salon (website)") reported that Cotton falsely claimed in campaign ads and videos from 2011 to 2014 that he had served in Iraq and Afghanistan and earned a Bronze Star as a U.S. Army Ranger even though he did not serve in the Army's [75th Ranger Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/75th_Ranger_Regiment "75th Ranger Regiment").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-Salon-14)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-dissemble-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-Wade-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-lockwood-24)[Fact-checking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fact-checking "Fact-checking") site [Snopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snopes "Snopes") rated Salon's reporting as true.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-25) In response to the article, Democratic congressman [Jason Crow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Crow "Jason Crow"), who served in the 75th Ranger Regiment, criticized Cotton for calling himself a Ranger. A spokesperson for Cotton said, "To be clear, as he's stated many times, Senator Cotton graduated from Ranger School, earned the Ranger Tab, and served a combat tour with the 101st Airborne, not the 75th Ranger Regiment."[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-26) As the Salon story garnered widespread attention, Cotton's spokeswoman recommended that the _[Arkansas Democrat-Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas\_Democrat-Gazette "Arkansas Democrat-Gazette")_ talk to retired [Command Sergeant Major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Command_Sergeant_Major "Command Sergeant Major") Rick Merritt, a former regimental sergeant major of the 75th Ranger Regiment, who said that Cotton is "100% a Ranger. He will always be a Ranger. It's unfair. It's almost slanderous."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-lockwood-24)

In an article on the controversy, _[Business Insider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business\_Insider "Business Insider")_ wrote, "[w]hile the distinction [between being a "Ranger" and attending Ranger School] is rarely brought up outside of military circles, it has been fiercely debated among veterans and encapsulates the nuances of military titles."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-27)

Cotton dismissed allegations that he had falsified his military record as politically motivated. "I graduated from the Ranger School, I wore the Ranger tab in combat with the 101st Airborne in Iraq. This is not about my military record. This is about my politics."[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-28)

## U.S. House of Representatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: U.S. House of Representatives")]

Shortly after Cotton's [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan "Afghanistan") deployment ended, he was introduced to [Chris Chocola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Chocola "Chris Chocola"), a former congressman and the president of [Club for Growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_for_Growth "Club for Growth"), a Republican [political action committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_action_committee "Political action committee") that became one of Cotton's top contributors.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-superstar-4) Cotton considered a run against incumbent Democratic U.S. senator [Blanche Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanche_Lincoln "Blanche Lincoln") in [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_States_Senate_election_in_Arkansas "2010 United States Senate election in Arkansas") but declined due to lack of donors and believing it was premature.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-gitom-5)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-29)

Cotton began his campaign for Congress in [Arkansas's 4th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas's_4th_congressional_district "Arkansas's 4th congressional district") in 2011 and had planned to run before [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") incumbent [Mike Ross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Ross_(politician) "Mike Ross (politician)") decided not to seek reelection.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-superstar-4)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-Joseph-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-auto-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-32)

Beth Anne Rankin, the 2010 Republican nominee, and John David Cowart, who was backed by Louisiana businessman and philanthropist [Edgar Cason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Cason?action=edit&redlink=1 "Edgar Cason (page does not exist)"), were the only other Republican candidates in the race after Marcus Richmond dropped out in February 2012.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-gitom-5) In the May 22 primary, Cotton won the Republican nomination with 57.6% of the vote; Rankin finished second with 37.1%.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-arkansas2012-35)

The [Club for Growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_for_Growth "Club for Growth") endorsed Cotton.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-36) Of the $2.2 million Cotton raised for his campaign, Club for Growth donors accounted for $315,000 and were his largest supporters.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-superstar-4) Senator [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain "John McCain") also endorsed him.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-37) Cotton was supported by both the [Tea Party movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_Party_movement "Tea Party movement") and the Republican establishment.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-39)

The first, [Jay Dickey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Dickey "Jay Dickey"), held it from 1993 to 2001, during the presidency of [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton"), whose residence was in the district.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-40) On January 3, 2013, Cotton was sworn into the House of Representatives by [Speaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Speaker_of_the_House "United States Speaker of the House")[John Boehner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Boehner "John Boehner").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-41)

### Tenure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Tenure")]

As a freshman, Cotton became a vocal opponent of the Obama administration's foreign and domestic policies. He voted for [an act to eliminate the 2013 statutory pay adjustment for federal employees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Act_to_eliminate_the_2013_statutory_pay_adjustment_for_Federal_employees "An Act to eliminate the 2013 statutory pay adjustment for Federal employees"), which prevented a 0.5% pay increase for all federal workers from taking effect in February 2013.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-42) Cotton voted against the [2013 Farm Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Agriculture_Reform_and_Risk_Management_Act_of_2013 "Federal Agriculture Reform and Risk Management Act of 2013") over concerns about waste and fraud in the [Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supplemental_Nutrition_Assistance_Program "Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program"), voting later that month to strip funding from that program.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-43) He also voted against the revised measure, the [Agricultural Act of 2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricultural_Act_of_2014 "Agricultural Act of 2014"),[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-44) which expanded crop insurance and a price floor for rice farmers.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-46)

Cotton accused Obama of presenting a "false choice" between the [Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Comprehensive_Plan_of_Action "Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action") and war. Cotton was also criticized in some media outlets for underestimating what successful military action against Iran would entail.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-npr-47) Cotton said, "the president is trying to make you think it would be 150,000 heavy mechanized troops on the ground in the Middle East again as we saw in Iraq. That's simply not the case." Drawing a comparison to President Clinton's actions in 1998 during the [Bombing of Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Iraq_(1998) "Bombing of Iraq (1998)"), he elaborated: "Several days' air and naval bombing against Iraq's weapons of mass destruction facilities for exactly the same kind of behavior. For interfering with weapons inspectors and for disobeying Security Council resolutions."[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-npr-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-48) On July 21, 2015, Cotton and [Mike Pompeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pompeo "Mike Pompeo") claimed to have uncovered the existence of secret side agreements between Iran and the [International Atomic Energy Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Atomic_Energy_Agency "International Atomic Energy Agency") (IAEA) on procedures for inspection and verification of Iran's nuclear activities under the JCPOA. Obama administration officials acknowledged the existence of agreements between Iran and the IAEA on the inspection of sensitive military sites, but denied that they were "secret side deals", calling them standard practice in crafting arms-control pacts and saying the administration had provided information about them to Congress.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-50)

On August 6, 2013, Cotton announced he would challenge Democratic incumbent [Mark Pryor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Pryor "Mark Pryor") for his seat in the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-52)[Stuart Rothenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Rothenberg "Stuart Rothenberg") of _[Roll Call](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roll\_Call "Roll Call")_ called Pryor the most vulnerable senator seeking reelection in 2014.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-53) Cotton was endorsed by the conservative [Club for Growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_for_Growth "Club for Growth") PAC,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-56) Senator [Marco Rubio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Rubio "Marco Rubio"),[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-57) the [National Federation of Independent Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Federation_of_Independent_Business "National Federation of Independent Business"),[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-58) and former presidential candidate [Mitt Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney "Mitt Romney"), who campaigned for Cotton.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-60) The [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") called the race for Cotton immediately after the polls closed;[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-61) he received 56.5% of the vote to Pryor's 39.4%.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-62) Cotton was sworn into office on January 6, 2015.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-63)

As a U.S. senator, Cotton has received multiple death threats. In 2018, Adam Albrett of [Fairfax County, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax_County,_Virginia "Fairfax County, Virginia") was arrested for "faxing death threats" against President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") and members of Congress, including Cotton. Police traced the fax to Albrett using the phone number in the fax header.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-64)

In October 2019, local authorities charged James Powell, a 43-year-old Arkansas resident, with "first-degree terroristic threatening" after an investigation by [U.S. Capitol Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Capitol_Police "United States Capitol Police") and the [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation"). The felony charge carries a maximum six-year prison sentence and a $10,000 fine. Powell also threatened Arkansas Representative [Rick Crawford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Crawford_(politician) "Rick Crawford (politician)") with death.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-66) In January 2020, 78-year-old Henry Edward Goodloe was sentenced to two years' probation for sending Cotton a threatening letter and a package containing white powder. Goodloe admitted to mailing an envelope containing white powder to Cotton's office, with a note stating, "You ignored me. Maybe this will get your attention." The Senate mail facility intercepted the letter, which included Goodloe's home address, and alerted a hazardous-response team, which determined the powder was unbleached flour and starch.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-67)

#### 2020

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: 2020")]

See also: [2020 United States Senate election in Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_Senate_election_in_Arkansas "2020 United States Senate election in Arkansas")

Cotton was reelected, defeating [Libertarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarian_Party_(United_States) "Libertarian Party (United States)") challenger Ricky Dale Harrington Jr. Though Cotton outperformed President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") in the [concurrent presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Arkansas "2020 United States presidential election in Arkansas") by 4.1%, the election saw an [undervote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undervote "Undervote") of 26,000 compared to the presidential election. Harrington's 33.5% finish is the best ever for a Libertarian candidate in a U.S. Senate election by vote percentage, surpassing the previous record set in 2016 in [Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_Senate_election_in_Alaska "2016 United States Senate election in Alaska"),[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-69) and also by total number of votes (399,390, surpassing the previous record of 369,807 set by Michael Cloud in [Massachusetts in 2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_United_States_Senate_election_in_Massachusetts "2002 United States Senate election in Massachusetts")). Per exit polls, this largely appears to be due to many Democrats voting for Harrington as there was no Democratic candidate on the ballot (82% of Democratic voters backed Harrington).[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-70)

#### Cassandra Butts nomination

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Cassandra Butts nomination")]

In February 2015, Obama renominated [Cassandra Butts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassandra_Butts "Cassandra Butts"), a former White House lawyer, to be the [United States ambassador to the Bahamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_Bahamas "List of ambassadors of the United States to the Bahamas"). Her nomination was blocked by several senators. First, [Ted Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Cruz "Ted Cruz") placed a blanket hold on all U.S. State Department nominees.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-Butts-72) Cotton specifically blocked the nominations of Butts and ambassador nominees to Sweden and Norway after the Secret Service leaked private information about a fellow member of Congress, although that issue was unrelated to those nominees. Cotton eventually released his hold on the nominees to Sweden and Norway, but kept his hold on Butts's nomination.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-Butts-72)

Butts told _New York Times_ columnist [Frank Bruni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Bruni "Frank Bruni") that she had gone to see Cotton about his objections to her nomination and said he had told her that because he knew that Obama and Butts were friends, it was a way to "inflict special pain on the president", Bruni said. Cotton's spokeswoman did not dispute Butts's characterization. Butts died on May 26, 2016, still awaiting a Senate vote.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-Butts-72)

Kelly") as [U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Homeland_Security "United States Secretary of Homeland Security").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-trumpism-9) Bannon told _The New Yorker_ in November 2017, "Next to Trump, he's the elected official who gets it the most—the economic nationalism. Cotton was the one most supportive of us, up front and behind the scenes, from the beginning. He understands that the Washington élite—this permanent political class of both parties ... needs to be shattered." In the same article, [Karl Rove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Rove "Karl Rove"), a senior figure in the [George W. Bush administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_George_W._Bush "Presidency of George W. Bush"), said Cotton was a more consensual figure than someone like Bannon.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-trumpism-9)

In a [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN") interview shortly after the [2016 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election "2016 United States presidential election"), Cotton denied that [waterboarding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterboarding "Waterboarding") is a form of [torture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torture "Torture"). He said "tough calls" such as allowing it were an option Trump was ready to take: "If experienced intelligence officials come to the President of the United States and say we think this terrorist has critical information and we need to obtain it and this is the only way we can obtain it—it's a tough call. But the presidency is a tough job. And if you're not ready to make those tough calls, you shouldn't seek the office. Donald Trump's a pretty tough guy, and he's ready to make those tough calls". During his 2016 presidential campaign, Trump said the United States should resume the use of waterboarding.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-75)

In September 2020, Trump shortlisted Cotton as a potential Supreme Court nominee, but ultimately chose [Amy Coney Barrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amy_Coney_Barrett "Amy Coney Barrett") instead.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-77) With less than two months to the next presidential election, Cotton supported an immediate Senate vote on Trump's nominee to fill the Supreme Court vacancy caused by Justice [Ruth Bader Ginsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Bader_Ginsburg "Ruth Bader Ginsburg")'s death. In March 2016, Cotton refused to consider Obama's Supreme Court nominee during a presidential election year, providing his rationale with these questions: "Why would we cut off the national debate on the next justice? Why would we squelch the voice of the populace? Why would we deny the voters a chance to weigh in on the makeup of the Supreme Court?"[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-78)

In early January 2021, Cotton announced he would not support any [attempts to overturn the 2020 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attempts_to_overturn_the_2020_United_States_presidential_election "Attempts to overturn the 2020 United States presidential election") during the joint congressional certification of Electoral College results on January 6, 2021.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-79)

## Political positions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Political positions")]

Cotton is considered politically conservative. The American Conservative Union's Center for Legislative Accountability gives him a lifetime rating of 86.06.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-85)

### 2023 Omnibus Appropriations Bill

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: 2023 Omnibus Appropriations Bill")]

Cotton was one of 18 Republican senators to vote for the $1.7 trillion omnibus bill that former President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") criticized. The bill earmarked $45 billion more for [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine") to defend itself against [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"), but prohibited funding for more immigration barriers in the U.S. and did not raise border enforcement spending past current inflation levels.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-86)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-88)

### Race relations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Race relations")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Senator_of_Arkansas_Tom_Cotton_at_NH_FITN_2016_by_Michael_Vadon_08.jpg/250px-Senator_of_Arkansas_Tom_Cotton_at_NH_FITN_2016_by_Michael_Vadon_08.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Senator_of_Arkansas_Tom_Cotton_at_NH_FITN_2016_by_Michael_Vadon_08.jpg)

Senator Cotton at First in the Nation Townhall, [New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Hampshire "New Hampshire")

Cotton drew scrutiny for columns he wrote for _[The Harvard Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Harvard\_Crimson "The Harvard Crimson")_ about race relations in America, calling [Jesse Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Jackson "Jesse Jackson") and [Al Sharpton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Sharpton "Al Sharpton") "race-hustling charlatans" and saying race relations "would almost certainly improve if we stopped emphasizing race in our public life."[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-Roller_2013-89)

In 2016, Cotton rejected the claim that too many criminals are being jailed, that there is [over-incarceration in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incarceration_in_the_United_States "Incarceration in the United States"), as "Law enforcement is able to arrest or identify a likely perpetrator for only 19 percent of property crimes and 47 percent of violent crimes. If anything, we have an under-incarceration problem".[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-:0-90) Cotton said that reduced sentencing for felons would destabilize the United States, arguing that "I saw this in Baghdad. We've seen it again in Afghanistan."[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-:0-90)

In November 2018, while arguing against a bipartisan criminal justice reform bill, Cotton incorrectly said that there had been no hearings on the bill. PolitiFact stated Cotton had "ignored years of congressional debate and hearings on the general topics of the bill, as well as the consideration and bipartisan passage of largely similar bills at the House committee level, by the full House, and by the Senate Judiciary Committee."[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-91) Arguing against the bill in question, the [FIRST STEP Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIRST_STEP_Act "FIRST STEP Act"), Cotton asserted that "convicts of certain sex-related crimes could accrue credits making them eligible for supervised release or 'pre-release' to a [halfway house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halfway_house "Halfway house")". A spokesperson for [Mike Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Lee "Mike Lee") responded that "just because a federal offense is not on the specific list of ineligible offenses doesn't mean inmates who committed [a] non-specified offense will earn early release".[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-92) The bill passed 87–12 on December 18, 2018. Cotton voted against it.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-93)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Tom_Cotton_and_Brett_Kavanaugh.jpg/250px-Tom_Cotton_and_Brett_Kavanaugh.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tom_Cotton_and_Brett_Kavanaugh.jpg)

Tom Cotton and [Brett Kavanaugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brett_Kavanaugh "Brett Kavanaugh") in August 2018

Following the [murder of George Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_George_Floyd "Murder of George Floyd"), Cotton rejected the view that there is "[systemic racism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institutional_racism "Institutional racism") in the [criminal justice system in America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_and_crime_in_the_United_States "Race and crime in the United States")".[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-94) Amid the [ensuing protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Floyd_protests "George Floyd protests"), Cotton advocated on Twitter that the military be used to support police, and to give "no quarter for insurrectionists, anarchists, rioters, and looters".[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-95) In the military, the term '[no quarter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_quarter "No quarter")' refers to the killing of lawfully surrendering combatants, which is a [war crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_crime "War crime") under the [Geneva Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva_Conventions "Geneva Conventions"). Cotton subsequently said he was using the "colloquial" version of the phrase and cited examples of Democrats and the mainstream media using it.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-96)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-97)

A few days later, _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ published an opinion piece by Cotton titled "Send in the Troops", arguing for the deployment of federal troops to counter looting and rioting in major American cities. Dozens of _Times_ staff members sharply criticized the decision to publish Cotton's article, calling its rhetoric dangerous.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-98)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-99) Following the negative response from staffers, the _Times_ responded by saying the piece went through a "rushed editorial process" that would be reexamined.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-Ellefson_2020-100) Editorial page editor [James Bennet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Bennet_(journalist) "James Bennet (journalist)") resigned days later.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-101) Cotton criticized the _Times_ for retracting his piece, saying, "_The New York Times_ editorial page editor and owner defended it in public statements but then they totally surrendered to a woke child mob from their own newsroom that apparently gets triggered if they're presented with any opinion contrary to their own, as opposed to telling the woke children in their newsroom this is the workplace, not a social justice seminar on campus".[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-102)

#### Statements about slavery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Statements about slavery")]

In July 2020, Cotton introduced the Saving American History Act of 2020, proposed legislation preventing the use of federal tax dollars for the teaching of [The 1619 Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_1619_Project "The 1619 Project"), an initiative of _The New York Times_.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-Lockwood_2020-103)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-104)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-105) In an interview with the _[Arkansas Democrat-Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas\_Democrat-Gazette "Arkansas Democrat-Gazette")_, Cotton said of slavery, "As the Founding Fathers said, it was the necessary evil upon which the union was built, but the union was built in a way, as Lincoln said, to put slavery on the course to its ultimate extinction."[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-106)[Joshua D. Rothman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_D._Rothman "Joshua D. Rothman"), a history professor at the University of Alabama, responded that slavery was neither "necessary" nor on the way to "extinction" when America was founded, because it "was a choice defended or accepted by most white Americans for generations, and it expanded dramatically between the Revolution and the Civil War".[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-107)

1619 Project director [Nikole Hannah-Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikole_Hannah-Jones "Nikole Hannah-Jones") tweeted: "If chattel slavery—heritable, generational, permanent, race-based slavery where it was legal to rape, torture, and sell human beings for profit—were a 'necessary evil' as [Tom Cotton] says, it's hard to imagine what cannot be justified if it is a means to an end." Cotton responded, "more lies from the debunked 1619 Project" and said he was "not endorsing or justifying slavery" because he was relaying what he believed were the "views of the Founders".[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-108) Georgetown University historian Adam Rothman said Cotton's phrase is "really a kind of shorthand way of describing the complex set of attitudes of the founding generation and it's not really accurate."[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-:2-109) "Of course slavery is an evil institution in all its forms, at all times in America's past, or around the world today", Cotton said on [Fox News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_News "Fox News") on July 27.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-:2-109)

### Gun laws

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Gun laws")]

In January 2019, Cotton was one of 31 Republican senators to cosponsor the Constitutional Concealed Carry Reciprocity Act, a bill introduced by [John Cornyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cornyn "John Cornyn") and [Ted Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Cruz "Ted Cruz") that would grant individuals with concealed carry privileges in their home state the right to exercise this right in any other state with concealed carry laws while concurrently abiding by that state's laws.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-112)

Cotton has an A grade from the [National Rifle Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rifle_Association "National Rifle Association") (NRA), which endorsed him in the 2014 election. The NRA's Chris W. Cox said, "Tom Cotton will always stand up for the values and freedoms of Arkansas gun owners and sportsmen."[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-113) In response to the [2017 Las Vegas shooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Las_Vegas_shooting "2017 Las Vegas shooting"), Cotton said the weapon sounded like a belt-fed machine gun and that he did not believe any new gun control legislation would have prevented the shooting.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-114) When it was later established that the shooter had used semi-automatic rifles with a [bump stock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bump_stock "Bump stock") attachment, he said he was "willing to entertain" regulation of bump stocks.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-115) In June 2022, Cotton introduced the "Stop Gun Criminals Act", which sought to increase minimum sentences for existing offenses but provided no new regulation.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-116)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-117) In May 2022, People.com listed Cotton as one of the U.S. lawmakers who had received the most funding from the NRA.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-118)

### Immigration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Immigration")]

Cotton's 2012 campaign website stated, "We cannot afford to grant illegal aliens amnesty or a so-called 'earned path to citizenship'."[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-119)

In July 2013, after the Senate's bipartisan [Gang of Eight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gang_of_Eight_(immigration) "Gang of Eight (immigration)") passed the [Border Security, Economic Opportunity, and Immigration Modernization Act of 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Security,_Economic_Opportunity,_and_Immigration_Modernization_Act_of_2013 "Border Security, Economic Opportunity, and Immigration Modernization Act of 2013"), an immigration reform proposal, House Republicans held a closed-door meeting to decide whether to bring the bill to a vote.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-flank-120) Budget Committee chairman [Paul Ryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Ryan "Paul Ryan") spoke at one podium arguing for its passage;[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-newyorker16-121) Cotton spoke at another arguing against it, even exchanging terse comments with Speaker Boehner.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-flank-120) The House decided to not consider the bill.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-newyorker16-121) Cotton supported Trump's 2017 [Executive Order 13769](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_13769 "Executive Order 13769") prohibiting immigration from seven predominantly Muslim countries.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-122)

On February 7, 2017, in the presence of President Trump, Cotton and Senator [David Perdue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Perdue "David Perdue") proposed a new immigration bill, the [RAISE Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reforming_American_Immigration_for_Strong_Employment_Act "Reforming American Immigration for Strong Employment Act"), which would limit the family route or [chain migration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_migration "Chain migration"). The bill would set a limit on the number of refugees offered residency at 50,000 a year and would remove the [Diversity Immigrant Visa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diversity_Immigrant_Visa "Diversity Immigrant Visa"). Senators [Lindsey Graham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindsey_Graham "Lindsey Graham") and [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain "John McCain") expressed opposition to the bill.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-123)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-124)

Cotton, a supporter of Trump on immigration, was present at a January 11, 2018, meeting at which Trump is alleged to have called [Haiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haiti "Haiti") and [African nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sovereign_states_and_dependent_territories_in_Africa "List of sovereign states and dependent territories in Africa") "shithole countries".[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-NBC20180112-125)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-Slate20180124-126) Cotton and Senator David Perdue said in a joint statement that "we do not recall the President saying these comments specifically".[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-twsCNN494-127) In a statement, the White House did not deny that Trump had made the comment, although Trump did in a tweet the following day.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-NBC20180112-125)_[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Post "The Washington Post")_ reported that Cotton and Perdue told the White House they heard "shithouse" rather than "shithole".[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-Wash_Post_2018-01-15-128) Cotton reiterated on CBS's _Face The Nation_, "I certainly didn't hear what Senator Durbin has said repeatedly". "Senator Durbin has a history of misrepresenting what happens in White House meetings, though, so perhaps we shouldn't be surprised by that", Cotton added.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-129)_[Slate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slate\_(magazine) "Slate (magazine)")_ magazine asserted that Cotton was referring to a misquotation [Dick Durbin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Durbin "Dick Durbin") made of a 2013 gathering at the Obama White House at which Durbin was not present, nor had he claimed to be present. Durbin was not the only person at the meeting to confirm Trump's words; another was Lindsey Graham.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-Slate20180124-126)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-130)

In December 2018, Cotton placed a senatorial hold on [H.R.7164](https://www.congress.gov/bill/115th-congress/house-bill/7164) – A Bill to add Ireland to the E-3 Non-immigrant Visa Program.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-131) The bill did not create new non-immigrant visas, but rather allowed Irish college graduates to apply for any surplus E-3 visas in Specialty Occupations that had gone unused by Australians within their annual cap of 10,500.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-132) The bipartisan bill had passed the House of Representatives on November 28, 2018, and had also received the backing of the Trump administration. Because of Cotton's hold, it did not reach the Senate floor for consideration.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-133)

Cotton's immigration positions have led to protests at his Washington office. In January 2018, five demonstrators were arrested for obstructing his office while they were protesting his position on [Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deferred_Action_for_Childhood_Arrivals "Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals"). They were released after paying a $50 fine.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-134)

In February 2021, in a speech at [CPAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Political_Action_Conference "Conservative Political Action Conference"), Cotton criticized the Democrats' and Joe Biden's immigration policies. Cotton claimed, "They have halted deportations for all illegal aliens. Murderers, rapists, terrorists, MS-13 gang members are not being deported." [PolitiFact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PolitiFact "PolitiFact") rated Cotton's claim as "False" and elaborated that the "Biden administration ordered a 100-day deportation pause, but it did not apply to criminals such as murderers, rapists, terrorists, or gang members."[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-135)

During a February 5, 2015, [Senate Armed Services Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Armed_Services "United States Senate Committee on Armed Services") hearing, Cotton called for housing more prisoners at [Guantanamo Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guantanamo_Bay_detention_camp "Guantanamo Bay detention camp") instead of closing it. #### China

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Cotton&action=edit&section=39 "Edit section: China")]

In 2018, Cotton was a cosponsor of the Countering the Chinese Government and Communist Party's Political Influence Operations Act, a bill introduced by [Marco Rubio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Rubio "Marco Rubio") and [Catherine Cortez Masto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Cortez_Masto "Catherine Cortez Masto") that would grant the U.S. secretary of state and the director of national intelligence (DNI) the authority to create an interagency task force with the purpose of examining attempts by China to influence the U.S. and key allies.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-174)

In August 2018, Cotton and 16 other lawmakers urged the Trump administration to impose sanctions under the [Global Magnitsky Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnitsky_Act#Global_Magnitsky_Act "Magnitsky Act") against [Chinese officials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_China "Communist Party of China") who are responsible for [human rights violations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang_re-education_camps "Xinjiang re-education camps") in western [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")'s [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang") region targeting the [Uyghur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs") ethnic minority.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-175) They wrote in a bipartisan letter, "The detention of as many as a million or more Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim ethnic minorities in 'political reeducation' centers or camps requires a tough, targeted, and global response".[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-176)

In February 2019, Cotton was one of the group of Senate Republicans who signed a letter to [Speaker of the House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives "Speaker of the United States House of Representatives")[Nancy Pelosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi "Nancy Pelosi") requesting that Pelosi invite [President of Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Taiwan "President of Taiwan")[Tsai Ing-wen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsai_Ing-wen "Tsai Ing-wen") to address a joint meeting of Congress. The request came amid heightened tensions between the U.S. and China and was expected to anger Chinese leadership if granted.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-177)

In May 2019, when asked about the impact of tariffs on farmers in Arkansas, Cotton said there would be "some sacrifices on the part of Americans, I grant you that, but I also would say that sacrifice is pretty minimal compared to the sacrifices that our soldiers make overseas that are fallen heroes that are laid to rest in Arlington make", and that farmers were willing to make sacrifices in order for the U.S. to fend off Chinese attempts to displace the U.S. globally.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-178)

In May 2019, Cotton was a cosponsor of the South China Sea and East China Sea Sanctions Act, a bipartisan bill reintroduced by [Marco Rubio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Rubio "Marco Rubio") and [Ben Cardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Cardin "Ben Cardin") that was intended to disrupt China's consolidation or expansion of its claims of jurisdiction over both the sea and air space in disputed zones in the South China Sea.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-179)

In July 2019, Cotton and Senator [Chris Van Hollen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Van_Hollen "Chris Van Hollen") were the primary sponsors of the Defending America's 5G Future Act, a bill that would prevent Huawei from being removed from the "entity list" of the Commerce Department without an act of Congress and authorize Congress to block administration waivers for U.S. companies to do business with Huawei. The bill would also codify Trump's executive order from the previous May that empowered his administration to block foreign tech companies deemed a national security threat from conducting business in the United States.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-180)

In April 2020, Cotton said that Chinese students in the United States should be restricted to studying the humanities and banned from studying science-related fields. In an interview with Fox News, he said, "It is a scandal to me that we have trained so many of the Chinese Communist Party's brightest minds."[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-181)[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-182)

On August 10, 2020, the Chinese government [sanctioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_sanctions "Chinese sanctions") Cotton and 10 other Americans for "behaving badly on Hong Kong-related issues".[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-183)

In February 2021, Cotton released a report, "Beat China: Targeted Decoupling and the Economic Long War", that called for the U.S. to sever most economic ties with China and invest in scientific, technological, and manufacturing fields China is ahead in.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-:3-184) The report called for economic restrictions on China despite the costs, saying the "costs of targeted decoupling with China pale in comparison to the costs of passivity"; more sanctions against theft of U.S. intellectual property, controls on U.S. technologies exported to China; barring "Chinese nationals in graduate and post-graduate programs in the United States from studying or conducting research in sensitive science, technology, engineering, and mathematics fields"; and expanded trade relations with allied countries to mitigate the impact of decoupling with China. In a speech detailing the report, Cotton said, "We need to beat this evil empire and consign the Chinese Communists ... to the ash heap of history".[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-:3-184)

In March 2023, Cotton and Senator [Katie Britt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katie_Britt "Katie Britt") introduced the Not One More Inch or Acre Act, which would ban any Chinese national or Chinese entity from owning American land.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-185) Cotton and Britt introduced the bill again in January 2025.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cotton#cite_note-186)

In January 2024, Cotton questioned TikTok CEO [Shou Zi Chew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shou_Zi_Chew "Shou Zi Chew") during a Senate hearing on child safety on social media, repeatedly asking Shou whether he was a member of the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party").
