Carper is considered a [moderate Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Democrats_(United_States) "New Democrats (United States)").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-32) He has a 13% conservative rating from the [American Conservative Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Conservative_Union "American Conservative Union").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-34) Carper voted for the [Budget Control Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budget_Control_Act_of_2011 "Budget Control Act of 2011"), against cut, cap and balance, for debt increase, for debt ceiling increase, for [debt limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debt_limit "Debt limit") increase, for the stimulus, for TARP, for the [Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patient_Protection_and_Affordable_Care_Act "Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act"), for [SCHIP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_Health_Insurance_Program "Children's Health Insurance Program"), for DREAM, and for the Immigration Reform Act of 2006.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-35)

### Abortion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Abortion")]

Carper has a mixed record on [abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion "Abortion") issues. In 2003, he was one of 17 Democrats who broke with the majority of their party by voting to ban [partial-birth abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial-birth_abortion "Partial-birth abortion").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-36) He also voted against banning abortion after 20 weeks of pregnancy, but voted to ban the use of federal funds for abortion.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-37) In 2018, he opposed President Trump's proposal to defund [Planned Parenthood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_Parenthood "Planned Parenthood").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-38) Carper was given a 50% rating by [NARAL Pro-Choice America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NARAL_Pro-Choice_America "NARAL Pro-Choice America"), indicating a mixed record on abortion, according to their scoring, and a 25% rating from the [anti-abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-abortion "Anti-abortion")[National Right to Life Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Right_to_Life_Committee "National Right to Life Committee").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-39) After [_Roe v. Wade_ was overturned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobbs_v._Jackson_Women's_Health_Organization "Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization") in June 2022, he said the decision was "unconscionably cruel and wrong" and that it was a "dark day for our country and our Constitution."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-40)

### Foreign policy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Foreign policy")]

In April 2019, Carper was one of 34 senators to sign a letter to President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") encouraging him "to listen to members of your own Administration and reverse a decision that will damage our national security and aggravate conditions inside Central America", asserting that Trump had "consistently expressed a flawed understanding of U.S. foreign assistance" since becoming president and that he was "personally undermining efforts to promote U.S. national security and economic prosperity" through preventing the use of Fiscal Year 2018 national security funding. The senators argued that foreign assistance to Central American countries created less migration to the U.S., citing the funding's helping to improve conditions in those countries.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-41)

In January 2024, Carper voted against a resolution, proposed by [Bernie Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders"), to apply the [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_violations_against_Palestinians_by_Israel "Human rights violations against Palestinians by Israel") provisions of the [Foreign Assistance Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Assistance_Act "Foreign Assistance Act") to [U.S. aid to Israel's military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_support_for_Israel_in_the_Gaza_war "United States support for Israel in the Gaza war"). The proposal was defeated, 72 to 11.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-42) In March 2024, Carper led a letter to the Biden administration urging the U.S. to recognize a "nonmilitarized" [Palestinian state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Palestine "State of Palestine") after the war in Gaza.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-43) This letter was signed by 19 Democratic senators who support a two-state solution to the [Israeli-Palestine conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_conflict "Israeli–Palestinian conflict").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-44)

### Gun law

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Gun law")]

Carper joined 23 other Senate Democrats in signing a letter supporting Obama taking executive action to reduce gun violence.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-45) In 2013, he voted to ban high-capacity magazines of over 10 bullets.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-46) In 2016, Carper participated in the [Chris Murphy gun control filibuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Murphy_gun_control_filibuster "Chris Murphy gun control filibuster").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-47) In response to the [2017 Las Vegas shooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Las_Vegas_shooting "2017 Las Vegas shooting"), Carper called for more gun laws, specifically background checks and mental health screenings.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-48)

In January 2019, Carper was one of 40 senators to introduce the Background Check Expansion Act, a bill that would require background checks for either the sale or transfer of all firearms including all unlicensed sellers. Exceptions to the bill's background check requirement included transfers between members of law enforcement, loaning firearms for either hunting or sporting events on a temporary basis, providing firearms as gifts to members of one's immediate family, firearms being transferred as part of an inheritance, or giving a firearm to another person temporarily for immediate self-defense.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-49)

### Finance and economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Finance and economy")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/UNDERMINE_PRESIDENT%E2%80%99S_CLEAN_POWER_PLAN_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-UNDERMINE_PRESIDENT%E2%80%99S_CLEAN_POWER_PLAN_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UNDERMINE_PRESIDENT%E2%80%99S_CLEAN_POWER_PLAN_(cropped).jpg)

Carper in 2015

He joined in the unsuccessful attempt to tie the [Bush tax cuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bush_tax_cuts "Bush tax cuts") to [deficit reduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_budget_deficit "Government budget deficit") and has supported additional funding for [school choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_choice "School choice") programs and [charter schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_schools "Charter schools"). He has also sought additional funding for railroad projects and for rail security. He strongly supported legislation to limit [class action lawsuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_action_lawsuits "Class action lawsuits") and to restrict [personal bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_bankruptcy "Personal bankruptcy"). In addition, he is a strong proponent of [free trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_trade "Free trade"). In 2012, Carper sponsored a bill, eventually passed and signed into law, that required government agencies to identify $125 billion in expected waste and fraud.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-50)

Carper and [George Voinovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Voinovich "George Voinovich") of [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio "Ohio") proposed a 25-cent raise in the federal gasoline tax; 10 cents would go to pay down the debt and the rest toward improving the nation's infrastructure. The measure was proposed in November 2010.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-51) The measure did not pass.

On May 14, 2011, _[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wall\_Street\_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")_ criticized a postal-bailout bill co-sponsored by Carper and [Susan Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Collins_(politician) "Susan Collins (politician)") (R-[Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine")). The bill would give $50–$75 billion to [USPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service"), and would underwrite pension obligations for retired postal workers. The bailout would cost three times the savings of the 2011 federal budget.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-52)

On August 1, 2019, the Senate passed a bipartisan budget deal that raised spending over current levels by $320 billion and lifted the debt ceiling for the following two years in addition to forming a course for funding the government without the perceived fiscal brinkmanship of recent years. Carper joined [Joe Manchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Manchin "Joe Manchin") and Republicans [Mitt Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney "Mitt Romney") and [Rick Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Scott "Rick Scott") in issuing a statement asserting that "as former Governors, we were responsible for setting a budget each year that was fiscally responsible to fund our priorities. That's why today, we, as U.S. Senators, cannot bring ourselves to vote for this budget deal that does not put our country on a fiscally sustainable path."[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-53)

### Environment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Environment")]

Carper proposed the creation of a [National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park "National Park") in Delaware, the Coastal Heritage Park, in four locations along the [Delaware River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_River "Delaware River") and [Delaware Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_Bay "Delaware Bay"). In January 2009, Carper briefly chaired a [Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Environment_and_Public_Works "United States Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works") hearing on the [Tennessee Valley Authority's coal ash spill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Fossil_Plant_coal_fly_ash_slurry_spill "Kingston Fossil Plant coal fly ash slurry spill") in [Kingston, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston,_Tennessee "Kingston, Tennessee"). However, he did vote for [Keystone XL Pipeline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keystone_XL_Pipeline "Keystone XL Pipeline"), but has since expressed disappointment in that vote.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-54)

Carper supports the [EPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EPA "EPA") and [Clean Air Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clean_Air_Act_(United_States) "Clean Air Act (United States)") and blames states to the west of Delaware for its air pollution, calling them "America's tailpipe".[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-55)

### Housing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Housing")]

In April 2019, Carper was one of 41 senators to sign a bipartisan letter to the housing subcommittee praising the [Housing and Urban Development Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Housing_and_Urban_Development "United States Department of Housing and Urban Development")'s Section 4 Capacity Building program as authorizing "HUD to partner with national nonprofit community development organizations to provide education, training, and financial support to local community development corporations (CDCs) across the country" and expressing disappointment that President Trump's budget "has slated this program for elimination after decades of successful economic and community development." The senators wrote of their hope that the subcommittee would support continued funding for Section 4 in Fiscal Year 2020.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-56)

### Technology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Technology")]

Carper co-wrote the "Protecting Cyberspace as a National Asset Act of 2010"[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-57) introduced on June 19, 2010, by Senator [Joe Lieberman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Lieberman "Joe Lieberman") (Senator Susan Collins is the third co-author of this bill). The bill, which generated controversy and was dubbed by the American media as the "_[Kill switch bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet\_kill\_switch#Protecting\_Cyberspace\_as\_a\_National\_Asset\_Act\_of\_2010 "Internet kill switch")_", would grant the [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") emergency powers over the Internet. All three co-authors of the bill, however, issued a statement claiming that instead, the bill "[narrowed] existing broad Presidential authority to take over telecommunications networks".[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-58) Carper was quoted as saying that the bill "would create a National Center for Cybersecurity and Communications in the [Department of Homeland Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Homeland_Security "United States Department of Homeland Security"), with a Senate-confirmed director to oversee security of the federal government's computer networks. The center would also identify vulnerabilities and help secure key private networks – like utilities and communications systems – that, if attacked or commandeered by a foreign power or cyberterrorists, could result in the crippling of our economy."[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-59)

### Consumer regulations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Consumer regulations")]

In May 2010, Carper introduced an amendment to limit state regulators from enforcing consumer regulations on national banks and their subsidiaries. It would also remove a Senate legislative measure requiring the [Office of the Comptroller of the Currency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_the_Comptroller_of_the_Currency "Office of the Comptroller of the Currency") to find a "substantive standard" on regulation, before the office could move to preempt. The [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") opposed Carper's amendment. The amendment passed by a vote of 80–18.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-60)

### Employment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Employment")]

#### Jobs bill

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Jobs bill")]

On September 21, 2011, _[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wall\_Street\_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")_ noted that President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama")'s job-creation plans were drawing resistance from Senate Democrats. The article quoted Carper as saying, "I think the best jobs bill that can be passed is a comprehensive long-term deficit-reduction plan. That's better than everything else the president is talking about combined."[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-61)

#### Minimum wage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Minimum wage")]

In April 2014, the United States Senate debated the [Minimum Wage Fairness Act (S. 1737; 113th Congress)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_Wage_Fairness_Act_(S._1737;_113th_Congress) "Minimum Wage Fairness Act (S. 1737; 113th Congress)"). The bill would amend the [Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Labor_Standards_Act_of_1938 "Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938") (FLSA) to increase the [federal minimum wage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_wage_in_the_United_States "Minimum wage in the United States") for employees to $10.10 per hour over the course of a two-year period.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-62) The bill was strongly supported by President Barack Obama and many of the Democratic Senators, but strongly opposed by Republicans in the Senate and House.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Reidpunts-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-65) Carper said that he preferred legislation that would have a greater chance of becoming law, such as an increase to only $9 an hour.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Reidpunts-64)

On March 5, 2021, Carper voted against [Bernie Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders")'s amendment to include a [$15/hour minimum wage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fight_for_$15 "Fight for $15") in the [American Rescue Plan Act of 2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Rescue_Plan_Act_of_2021 "American Rescue Plan Act of 2021").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-66)

### LGBT rights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: LGBT rights")]

Carper signed a law as Governor defining "marriage as between a man and a woman," but he also voted as a Senator against the [Federal Marriage Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Marriage_Amendment "Federal Marriage Amendment"), a proposed constitutional amendment to ban [gay marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage "Same-sex marriage").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-67) He also voted against banning gay marriage again in 2006.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-68) In 2013, Carper announced that he now supports [same-sex marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage "Same-sex marriage").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-69)

### Iraq War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Iraq War")]

Carper voted yes on the 2002 [Iraq War Resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_Resolution "Iraq Resolution").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-70)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Carper has been married twice, first in 1978, to Diane Beverly Isaacs, a former [Miss Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Delaware "Miss Delaware"), who had two children by a previous marriage. They divorced in 1983. In a 1998 interview, Carper admitted, "I slapped my then-wife, Diane, during a heated argument," calling it a mistake.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-71)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Bowden-5) According to a 1982 [New York Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Post "New York Post") article, Carper hit Isaacs "so hard he gave her a black eye" and his wife's two children from a previous relationship "were slapped around and bruised by Carper for doing such things as leaving the family dog on the bed." Carper denied these claims.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Bowden-5)

Carper married Martha Ann Stacy in 1985. They have two children. The family are members of Westminster Presbyterian Church in [Wilmington, Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmington,_Delaware "Wilmington, Delaware").

Unlike most senators, who maintain residences in both [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), and in their home state, Carper commuted more than 100 miles by [Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak") train from his home in Wilmington to the [United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Capitol "United States Capitol"). He said this arrangement helped his family live a normal life despite his demanding, high-profile job.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-72) On May 12, 2015, he narrowly escaped injury when the train he took home [derailed and crashed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Philadelphia_train_derailment "2015 Philadelphia train derailment") in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") shortly after he debarked.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-73) In 2024, [Newark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark,_Delaware "Newark, Delaware") Train Station was renamed in his honor.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-74)

### Finances

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Finances")]

As of 2018, according to OpenSecrets.org, Carper's net worth was more than $5.7 million.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-net-worth-75)

In August 2023, [Congresstrading.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congresstrading.com "Congresstrading.com") tweeted that Carper, a senior member of the Senate Finance Committee, made an inverse Nasdaq [ETF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exchange-traded_fund "Exchange-traded fund") purchase, a [short sell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_sell "Short sell") option for investors looking to hedge against or profit from a decline in the index. The tweet questioned whether this was a conflict of interest for Carper.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Moorcraft_2023-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Congresstrading.com_tweet_2023-08-02-77)

**Thomas Richard Carper** (born January 23, 1947) is an American politician and former military officer who served from 2001 to 2025 as a [United States senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") from [Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware "Delaware"). A member of the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), Carper served from 1983 to 1993 in the [United States House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") and from 1993 to 2001 as the 71st [governor of Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Delaware "List of governors of Delaware").

A native of [Beckley, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beckley,_West_Virginia "Beckley, West Virginia"), Carper graduated from [Ohio State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_State_University "Ohio State University") on an [NROTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NROTC "NROTC") scholarship. Serving as a [naval flight officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_flight_officer "Naval flight officer") in the [U.S. Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Navy "U.S. Navy") from 1968 until 1973, he flew the [P-3 Orion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-3_Orion "P-3 Orion") as a tactical coordinator and mission commander[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-1) and saw active duty in the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"). After leaving the active duty Navy, he remained in the [U.S. Naval Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Naval_Reserve "U.S. Naval Reserve") for another 18 years and eventually retired with the rank of [Captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(United_States) "Captain (United States)") (O-6). Upon receiving his [MBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Business_Administration "Master of Business Administration") from the [University of Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Delaware "University of Delaware") in 1975, Carper went to work for the state of Delaware in its economic development office. He was elected state treasurer, serving from 1977 to 1983 and leading the development of Delaware's first cash management system.

Encouraged by local politicians, Carper successfully ran for Delaware's only seat in the U.S. House of Representatives in 1982. He served five terms in the House, where he chaired the Subcommittee on Economic Stabilization. In 1992, he swapped positions with term-limited Republican Governor [Mike Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Castle "Mike Castle"), and the two were easily elected to each other's seats. Carper governed for two terms as a moderate, business-oriented [New Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Democrats_(United_States) "New Democrats (United States)"), following the lead of the two previous Republican governors.

Carper was elected to the U.S. Senate in [2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "2000 United States Senate election in Delaware"), defeating Republican incumbent [William Roth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Roth "William Roth"). He was reelected by landslides in [2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "2006 United States Senate election in Delaware"), [2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "2012 United States Senate election in Delaware"), and [2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "2018 United States Senate election in Delaware"). He served as one of four deputy Democratic whips, the chairman of the [Senate Environment and Public Works Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Environment_and_Public_Works "United States Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works") and on the [Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Homeland_Security_and_Governmental_Affairs "United States Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs") and the [Finance Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Finance "United States Senate Committee on Finance"). Carper was the senior senator in [Delaware's congressional delegation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware's_congressional_delegations "Delaware's congressional delegations") and the dean of the delegation. He was the last Vietnam War veteran to serve in the Senate.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Carper was born in Beckley, West Virginia, the son of Mary Jean (née Patton) and Wallace Richard Carper. He grew up in [Danville, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danville,_Virginia "Danville, Virginia"), and graduated from [Whetstone High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whetstone_High_School_(Columbus,_Ohio) "Whetstone High School (Columbus, Ohio)") in [Columbus, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio"). He then graduated from the [Ohio State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_State_University "Ohio State University") in 1968, where he was a midshipman in the [Naval ROTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_ROTC "Naval ROTC") and earned a [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") degree in [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics"). At Ohio State, Carper became a member of the Beta Phi Chapter of the [Delta Tau Delta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_Tau_Delta "Delta Tau Delta") fraternity. Carper earned an [MBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Business_Administration "Master of Business Administration") from the [University of Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Delaware "University of Delaware") in 1975.

## Early career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early career")]

Serving as a [Naval Flight Officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Flight_Officer "Naval Flight Officer") in the [U.S. Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Navy "U.S. Navy") from 1968 until 1973, he served three tours of duty in [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia") during the Vietnam War. He remained in the [U.S. Naval Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Naval_Reserve "U.S. Naval Reserve") as a [P-3 aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_P-3_Orion "Lockheed P-3 Orion") mission commander for another 18 years, stationed with [VP-66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VP-66 "VP-66") at [NAS Willow Grove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Willow_Grove "NAS Willow Grove") in Pennsylvania. He retired with the rank of [Captain (O-6)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(United_States_O-6) "Captain (United States O-6)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-2)

While in college at the Ohio State University, Carper worked on the presidential campaign of U.S. Senator [Eugene McCarthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_McCarthy "Eugene McCarthy"). In Delaware, he worked as the campaign treasurer for University of Delaware professor James R. Soles in his unsuccessful 1974 bid for the [U.S. House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._House_of_Representatives "U.S. House of Representatives").

After receiving his MBA degree in 1975, Carper went to work for the State of Delaware's economic development office. In 1976, after developing good relationships with members of the state party leadership, he took out a $5,000 personal loan to fund his campaign to be Treasurer of Delaware. In the election, he defeated the favored Republican Party candidate, Theodore Jones. He served three terms, from January 18, 1977, through January 3, 1983, during which time he oversaw the development of Delaware's first cash management system.

## U.S. House of Representatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: U.S. House of Representatives")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/Tom_Carper_102nd_Congressional_portrait.jpg/250px-Tom_Carper_102nd_Congressional_portrait.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tom_Carper_102nd_Congressional_portrait.jpg)

Carper during his time in the House of Representatives

In 1982, U.S. Senator [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") and other prominent Democrats convinced Carper to run for Delaware's only seat in the U.S. House of Representatives. Incumbent Republican [Thomas B. Evans Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_B._Evans_Jr. "Thomas B. Evans Jr.") sought reelection, and although he had been caught in a compromising "association" on a golfing trip with the lobbyist Paula Parkinson, was still considered a strong candidate.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-3)

Carper was considered well-positioned until three weeks before Election Day, when the _[New York Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_York\_Post "New York Post")_ published an article claiming that the "dirtiest campaign in the country is being waged in tiny Delaware", which suggested that Carper had abused his wife and stepchildren. But when rumors spread that the story was "planted" by a supporter of Evans, Carper bounced back, with public opinion seeming to be that the allegations inappropriately exploited private issue.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-OnlyinDelaware-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Bowden-5) Carper and his wife both denied the allegations in 1982, but he later admitted to having slapped her. Carper defeated Evans.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-6)

Carper served five terms in the House. He won his second term in 1984, defeating Elise R. W. du Pont, the wife of retiring Governor [Pete du Pont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_du_Pont "Pete du Pont"). He then easily defeated Republicans Thomas S. Neuberger in 1986, James P. Krapf in 1988 and Ralph O. Williams in 1990. He was a member of the [U.S. House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._House_Committee_on_Financial_Services "U.S. House Committee on Financial Services") and the [U.S. House Committee on Merchant Marine and Fisheries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._House_Committee_on_Transportation_and_Infrastructure "U.S. House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure"). He chaired the House Subcommittee on Economic Stabilization. In these positions, he worked to allow banks into the securities business and to discourage the dumping of sludge into the ocean.

During his years in the House, Carper sought to gain better control of Delaware's Democratic Party organization in hopes of someday becoming governor, focusing on heavily Democratic and populous [New Castle County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Castle_County,_Delaware "New Castle County, Delaware"). Its Democratic organization was controlled by Eugene T. Reed, a former ironworker and longtime party boss who was then among several politicians in both parties implicated in illegal money raising practices. To address this corruption and rescue the Democratic Party's reputation, Carper recruited Joseph E. Reardon, a [DuPont Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DuPont_Company "DuPont Company") chemist, as a candidate for New Castle County Democratic Party chairman. By early 1989, Reardon had been elected, replacing Reed at the head of a newly reformed party organization. In 1990, Carper defeated a Reed ally, Daniel D. Rappa, in the Democratic primary for U.S. representative.

## Governor of Delaware

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Governor of Delaware")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/President_Bill_Clinton_and_First_Lady_Hillary_Clinton_greet_guests_at_the_National_Governors_Association_Dinner_in_the_Blue_Room_of_the_White_House_%2818%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_Bill_Clinton_and_First_Lady_Hillary_Clinton_greet_guests_at_the_National_Governors_Association_Dinner_in_the_Blue_Room_of_the_White_House_(18)_(cropped).jpg)

Carper with President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") in January 1993

Republican Governor Michael Castle was [term-limited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Term_limit "Term limit") and unable to seek reelection in 1992. The result was what became known as "the Swap", with Castle seeking Carper's seat in the U.S. House of Representatives and Carper seeking the governorship. Neither faced substantive opposition for either post.

Carper defeated Republican B. Gary Scott and was elected governor. He served two terms. Carper positioned himself as a moderate, business-oriented governor, emphasizing economic development and business recruitment. This included the prevention of the closure of the [General Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Motors "General Motors") automobile operation near [Newport, Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport,_Delaware "Newport, Delaware"), and convincing pharmaceutical giant [AstraZeneca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AstraZeneca "AstraZeneca") to construct its new headquarters in the state.

Carper led an ongoing effort to reduce [income tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_tax_in_the_United_States "Income tax in the United States") rates, eliminate the [marriage penalty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_penalty "Marriage penalty") and [estate tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estate_tax "Estate tax"), cut the public [utility tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility_tax?action=edit&redlink=1 "Utility tax (page does not exist)"), and eliminate the [gross receipts tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_receipts_tax "Gross receipts tax") for many small businesses. Delaware's credit rating improved from among the worst in the nation to AAA. Carper also retained Castle's standards-based education programs. Other programs included a fully funded [Head Start program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Start_(program) "Head Start (program)") and a prescription-drug benefit for seniors.

Carper had high approval ratings, but was criticized by some old-line Democrats and union leaders.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-OnlyinDelaware-4)

As a tribute to Anne Marie Fahey, who had been a youth [mentor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mentorship "Mentorship") before her death, then-Governor Carper also became a mentor, and began actively promoting mentoring programs throughout Delaware's business community. As a result, by the end of his last term, Delaware held the highest per-capita ratio of youth mentors in the country. Carper also established the Delaware Mentoring Council to help sustain this legacy.

#### 2000

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2000")]

See also: [2000 United States Senate election in Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "2000 United States Senate election in Delaware")

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Thomas_Carper.jpg/250px-Thomas_Carper.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Thomas_Carper.jpg)

Carper in his early Senate career

Due to term limits, Carper had to retire as governor in 2000, and sought election to the U.S. Senate against incumbent Republican [William Roth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Roth "William Roth"), declaring his candidacy in September 1999.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-7) Some had concerns about Roth's age of 79, compared to Carper's relative youth. Roth started the campaign with a 2-to-1 spending advantage, but Carper went into the final month with more than $1 million on hand.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Globe-Oct-2000-8) He defeated Roth, 56% to 44%. Roth received more votes than Republican presidential candidate [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"), suggesting that the strength of the Democratic turnout for the presidential election was key in Carper's victory.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Some commentators attributed Roth's defeat to his age and health, as he collapsed twice during the campaign, once during a television interview and once during a campaign event.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Globe-Oct-2000-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-10)

#### 2006

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2006")]

See also: [2006 United States Senate election in Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "2006 United States Senate election in Delaware")

Carper sought reelection in 2006. He was unopposed in the Democratic primary and faced Republican nominee [Jan C. Ting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_C._Ting "Jan C. Ting"), a professor of law who had narrowly beaten airline pilot Michael D. Protack in the Republican primary. Carper was easily reelected, 67% to 27%.

#### 2012

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 2012")]

See also: [2012 United States Senate election in Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "2012 United States Senate election in Delaware")

As the 2012 election cycle began, a [Super PAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_action_committee "Political action committee") was created to oppose Carper's reelection campaign. _[The Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hill\_(newspaper) "The Hill (newspaper)")_ quoted [Patrick Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Davis_(politics) "Patrick Davis (politics)"), the custodian of records and agent for Renew Delaware as saying, "Tom Carper has served in the United States Senate for a long time and has been part of the downturn in our economy." _Delaware Politics_ noted that the election would be costly for the Republican candidate and that Carper was heavily favored to win a third term.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-11) A Carper spokesperson, Emily Spain, was quoted in _The Hill_ saying that Carper was successful in his previous campaigns "because he works hard, takes nothing for granted, and puts the needs and interests of Delaware first."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-12) Carper won the Democratic primary with 88% of the vote and faced off against the only Republican candidate who filed for the race, businessman [Kevin Wade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_L._Wade "Kevin L. Wade"). He was reelected with 66% of the vote.

#### 2018

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 2018")]

See also: [2018 United States Senate election in Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "2018 United States Senate election in Delaware")

In 2018, Carper sought his fourth Senate term.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-14) His campaign contributors included [DuPont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DuPont "DuPont"), his third-largest contributor since 2013. Between 2013 and 2018, he received $2.1 million from [political action committees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_action_committees "Political action committees").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-15) In the Democratic primary, Carper was challenged from the left by Kerri Evelyn Harris, a [US Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") Veteran, who, unlike Carper, supports a [single-payer healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-payer_healthcare "Single-payer healthcare").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-16) Carper won the primary with roughly 65% of the vote.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-17) It was his most competitive primary in recent history. In the general election, Carper defeated Republican nominee Rob Arlett, 60.0% to 37.8%.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-18)

#### 2024

On May 22, 2023, Carper announced that he would not seek reelection in 2024. In his press conference, Carper endorsed U.S. Representative [Lisa Blunt Rochester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Blunt_Rochester "Lisa Blunt Rochester").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-19)

Senator Carper retired from the United States Senate on January 3, 2025. He was the last remaining combat veteran of the Vietnam War serving in the U.S. Senate.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-21)

Carper served with the Democratic minority in the [108th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/108th_United_States_Congress "108th United States Congress") and [109th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/109th_United_States_Congress "109th United States Congress") Congresses and was part of the Democratic majority in the [110th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/110th_United_States_Congress "110th United States Congress") Congress. At the beginning of the [107th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/107th_United_States_Congress "107th United States Congress") Congress, the Democratic Party was in the minority, but later held the majority. Carper was a member of the moderate [Democratic Leadership Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Leadership_Council "Democratic Leadership Council") (DLC), of which he served as vice chair. In 2004, Carper became part of the Senate Democratic leadership. As a member of a four-person "Executive Committee", he was one of four deputy whips. [David Broder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Broder "David Broder") of _The Washington Post_ has called Carper "a notably effective and non-partisan leader, admired and trusted on both sides of the aisle."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-22)

During the [January 6 United States Capitol attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack "January 6 United States Capitol attack"), Carper said he did not support invoking the [Twenty-fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-fifth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Twenty-fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution") or [impeachment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_impeachment_in_the_United_States "Federal impeachment in the United States") of Trump.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-23) But hours later, he called on Trump to resign. He also called the attackers "domestic terrorists". That evening, he voted to certify the [2021 United States Electoral College vote count](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_United_States_Electoral_College_vote_count "2021 United States Electoral College vote count").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-24)

#### Third Circuit Vacancy During Senator Carper's Final Year in Office and Ultimate Conservative Shift

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Third Circuit Vacancy During Senator Carper's Final Year in Office and Ultimate Conservative Shift")]

Senator Carper, Senator [Coons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Coons "Chris Coons"), and President Biden declined to select a nominee for a judicial vacancy on the [Third Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Third_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit") in President Biden's home state of [Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware "Delaware") even though the vacancy was announced in May 2024, more than eight months before President Biden's four-year term in office ended.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Reuters-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Bloomberg_L.P-26) The White House's and the Delaware U.S. Senate delegation's decision not to fill the [Third Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Third_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit") vacancy in President Biden's home state of Delaware, along with President Biden's unsuccessful nomination of [Adeel A. Mangi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adeel_A._Mangi "Adeel A. Mangi") to another [Third Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Third_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit") vacancy, allowed President Trump to fill both seats in 2025 and flip the Third Circuit to a conservative majority.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Bloomberg_L.P-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-28) President Trump ultimately nominated [Jennifer Mascott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Mascott "Jennifer Mascott"), who had never taken the Delaware bar exam and was not licensed to practice law in Delaware,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-29) to the vacancy that Carper, Coons, and President Biden declined to fill in Biden's home state.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Reuters-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Bloomberg_L.P-26)

Carper is considered a [moderate Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Democrats_(United_States) "New Democrats (United States)").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-32) He has a 13% conservative rating from the [American Conservative Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Conservative_Union "American Conservative Union").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-34) Carper voted for the [Budget Control Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budget_Control_Act_of_2011 "Budget Control Act of 2011"), against cut, cap and balance, for debt increase, for debt ceiling increase, for [debt limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debt_limit "Debt limit") increase, for the stimulus, for TARP, for the [Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patient_Protection_and_Affordable_Care_Act "Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act"), for [SCHIP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_Health_Insurance_Program "Children's Health Insurance Program"), for DREAM, and for the Immigration Reform Act of 2006.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-35)

### Abortion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Abortion")]

Carper has a mixed record on [abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion "Abortion") issues. In 2003, he was one of 17 Democrats who broke with the majority of their party by voting to ban [partial-birth abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial-birth_abortion "Partial-birth abortion").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-36) He also voted against banning abortion after 20 weeks of pregnancy, but voted to ban the use of federal funds for abortion.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-37) In 2018, he opposed President Trump's proposal to defund [Planned Parenthood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_Parenthood "Planned Parenthood").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-38) Carper was given a 50% rating by [NARAL Pro-Choice America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NARAL_Pro-Choice_America "NARAL Pro-Choice America"), indicating a mixed record on abortion, according to their scoring, and a 25% rating from the [anti-abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-abortion "Anti-abortion")[National Right to Life Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Right_to_Life_Committee "National Right to Life Committee").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-39) After [_Roe v. Wade_ was overturned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobbs_v._Jackson_Women's_Health_Organization "Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization") in June 2022, he said the decision was "unconscionably cruel and wrong" and that it was a "dark day for our country and our Constitution."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-40)

### Foreign policy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Foreign policy")]

In April 2019, Carper was one of 34 senators to sign a letter to President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") encouraging him "to listen to members of your own Administration and reverse a decision that will damage our national security and aggravate conditions inside Central America", asserting that Trump had "consistently expressed a flawed understanding of U.S. foreign assistance" since becoming president and that he was "personally undermining efforts to promote U.S. national security and economic prosperity" through preventing the use of Fiscal Year 2018 national security funding. The senators argued that foreign assistance to Central American countries created less migration to the U.S., citing the funding's helping to improve conditions in those countries.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-41)

In January 2024, Carper voted against a resolution, proposed by [Bernie Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders"), to apply the [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_violations_against_Palestinians_by_Israel "Human rights violations against Palestinians by Israel") provisions of the [Foreign Assistance Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Assistance_Act "Foreign Assistance Act") to [U.S. aid to Israel's military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_support_for_Israel_in_the_Gaza_war "United States support for Israel in the Gaza war"). The proposal was defeated, 72 to 11.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-42) In March 2024, Carper led a letter to the Biden administration urging the U.S. to recognize a "nonmilitarized" [Palestinian state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Palestine "State of Palestine") after the war in Gaza.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-43) This letter was signed by 19 Democratic senators who support a two-state solution to the [Israeli-Palestine conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_conflict "Israeli–Palestinian conflict").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-44)

### Gun law

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Gun law")]

Carper joined 23 other Senate Democrats in signing a letter supporting Obama taking executive action to reduce gun violence.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-45) In 2013, he voted to ban high-capacity magazines of over 10 bullets.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-46) In 2016, Carper participated in the [Chris Murphy gun control filibuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Murphy_gun_control_filibuster "Chris Murphy gun control filibuster").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-47) In response to the [2017 Las Vegas shooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Las_Vegas_shooting "2017 Las Vegas shooting"), Carper called for more gun laws, specifically background checks and mental health screenings.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-48)

In January 2019, Carper was one of 40 senators to introduce the Background Check Expansion Act, a bill that would require background checks for either the sale or transfer of all firearms including all unlicensed sellers. Exceptions to the bill's background check requirement included transfers between members of law enforcement, loaning firearms for either hunting or sporting events on a temporary basis, providing firearms as gifts to members of one's immediate family, firearms being transferred as part of an inheritance, or giving a firearm to another person temporarily for immediate self-defense.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-49)

### Finance and economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Finance and economy")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/UNDERMINE_PRESIDENT%E2%80%99S_CLEAN_POWER_PLAN_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-UNDERMINE_PRESIDENT%E2%80%99S_CLEAN_POWER_PLAN_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UNDERMINE_PRESIDENT%E2%80%99S_CLEAN_POWER_PLAN_(cropped).jpg)

Carper in 2015

He joined in the unsuccessful attempt to tie the [Bush tax cuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bush_tax_cuts "Bush tax cuts") to [deficit reduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_budget_deficit "Government budget deficit") and has supported additional funding for [school choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_choice "School choice") programs and [charter schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_schools "Charter schools"). He has also sought additional funding for railroad projects and for rail security. He strongly supported legislation to limit [class action lawsuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_action_lawsuits "Class action lawsuits") and to restrict [personal bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_bankruptcy "Personal bankruptcy"). In addition, he is a strong proponent of [free trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_trade "Free trade"). In 2012, Carper sponsored a bill, eventually passed and signed into law, that required government agencies to identify $125 billion in expected waste and fraud.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-50)

Carper and [George Voinovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Voinovich "George Voinovich") of [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio "Ohio") proposed a 25-cent raise in the federal gasoline tax; 10 cents would go to pay down the debt and the rest toward improving the nation's infrastructure. The measure was proposed in November 2010.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-51) The measure did not pass.

On May 14, 2011, _[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wall\_Street\_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")_ criticized a postal-bailout bill co-sponsored by Carper and [Susan Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Collins_(politician) "Susan Collins (politician)") (R-[Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine")). The bill would give $50–$75 billion to [USPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service"), and would underwrite pension obligations for retired postal workers. The bailout would cost three times the savings of the 2011 federal budget.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-52)

On August 1, 2019, the Senate passed a bipartisan budget deal that raised spending over current levels by $320 billion and lifted the debt ceiling for the following two years in addition to forming a course for funding the government without the perceived fiscal brinkmanship of recent years. Carper joined [Joe Manchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Manchin "Joe Manchin") and Republicans [Mitt Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney "Mitt Romney") and [Rick Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Scott "Rick Scott") in issuing a statement asserting that "as former Governors, we were responsible for setting a budget each year that was fiscally responsible to fund our priorities. That's why today, we, as U.S. Senators, cannot bring ourselves to vote for this budget deal that does not put our country on a fiscally sustainable path."[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-53)

Carper proposed the creation of a [National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park "National Park") in Delaware, the Coastal Heritage Park, in four locations along the [Delaware River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_River "Delaware River") and [Delaware Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_Bay "Delaware Bay"). ### Housing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Housing")]

In April 2019, Carper was one of 41 senators to sign a bipartisan letter to the housing subcommittee praising the [Housing and Urban Development Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Housing_and_Urban_Development "United States Department of Housing and Urban Development")'s Section 4 Capacity Building program as authorizing "HUD to partner with national nonprofit community development organizations to provide education, training, and financial support to local community development corporations (CDCs) across the country" and expressing disappointment that President Trump's budget "has slated this program for elimination after decades of successful economic and community development." The senators wrote of their hope that the subcommittee would support continued funding for Section 4 in Fiscal Year 2020.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-56)

### Technology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Technology")]

Carper co-wrote the "Protecting Cyberspace as a National Asset Act of 2010"[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-57) introduced on June 19, 2010, by Senator [Joe Lieberman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Lieberman "Joe Lieberman") (Senator Susan Collins is the third co-author of this bill). The bill, which generated controversy and was dubbed by the American media as the "_[Kill switch bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet\_kill\_switch#Protecting\_Cyberspace\_as\_a\_National\_Asset\_Act\_of\_2010 "Internet kill switch")_", would grant the [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") emergency powers over the Internet. All three co-authors of the bill, however, issued a statement claiming that instead, the bill "[narrowed] existing broad Presidential authority to take over telecommunications networks".[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-58) Carper was quoted as saying that the bill "would create a National Center for Cybersecurity and Communications in the [Department of Homeland Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Homeland_Security "United States Department of Homeland Security"), with a Senate-confirmed director to oversee security of the federal government's computer networks. The center would also identify vulnerabilities and help secure key private networks – like utilities and communications systems – that, if attacked or commandeered by a foreign power or cyberterrorists, could result in the crippling of our economy."[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-59)

### Consumer regulations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Consumer regulations")]

In May 2010, Carper introduced an amendment to limit state regulators from enforcing consumer regulations on national banks and their subsidiaries. It would also remove a Senate legislative measure requiring the [Office of the Comptroller of the Currency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_the_Comptroller_of_the_Currency "Office of the Comptroller of the Currency") to find a "substantive standard" on regulation, before the office could move to preempt. #### Minimum wage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Minimum wage")]

In April 2014, the United States Senate debated the [Minimum Wage Fairness Act (S. 1737; 113th Congress)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_Wage_Fairness_Act_(S._1737;_113th_Congress) "Minimum Wage Fairness Act (S. 1737; 113th Congress)"). The bill would amend the [Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Labor_Standards_Act_of_1938 "Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938") (FLSA) to increase the [federal minimum wage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_wage_in_the_United_States "Minimum wage in the United States") for employees to $10.10 per hour over the course of a two-year period.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-62) The bill was strongly supported by President Barack Obama and many of the Democratic Senators, but strongly opposed by Republicans in the Senate and House.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Reidpunts-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-65) Carper said that he preferred legislation that would have a greater chance of becoming law, such as an increase to only $9 an hour.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Reidpunts-64)

On March 5, 2021, Carper voted against [Bernie Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders")'s amendment to include a [$15/hour minimum wage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fight_for_$15 "Fight for $15") in the [American Rescue Plan Act of 2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Rescue_Plan_Act_of_2021 "American Rescue Plan Act of 2021").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-66)

### LGBT rights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: LGBT rights")]

Carper signed a law as Governor defining "marriage as between a man and a woman," but he also voted as a Senator against the [Federal Marriage Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Marriage_Amendment "Federal Marriage Amendment"), a proposed constitutional amendment to ban [gay marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage "Same-sex marriage").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-67) He also voted against banning gay marriage again in 2006.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-68) In 2013, Carper announced that he now supports [same-sex marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage "Same-sex marriage").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-69)

### Iraq War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Iraq War")]

Carper voted yes on the 2002 [Iraq War Resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_Resolution "Iraq Resolution").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-70)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Carper has been married twice, first in 1978, to Diane Beverly Isaacs, a former [Miss Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Delaware "Miss Delaware"), who had two children by a previous marriage. They divorced in 1983. In a 1998 interview, Carper admitted, "I slapped my then-wife, Diane, during a heated argument," calling it a mistake.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-71)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Bowden-5) According to a 1982 [New York Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Post "New York Post") article, Carper hit Isaacs "so hard he gave her a black eye" and his wife's two children from a previous relationship "were slapped around and bruised by Carper for doing such things as leaving the family dog on the bed." Carper denied these claims.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Bowden-5)

Carper married Martha Ann Stacy in 1985. They have two children. The family are members of Westminster Presbyterian Church in [Wilmington, Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmington,_Delaware "Wilmington, Delaware").

Unlike most senators, who maintain residences in both [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), and in their home state, Carper commuted more than 100 miles by [Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak") train from his home in Wilmington to the [United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Capitol "United States Capitol"). He said this arrangement helped his family live a normal life despite his demanding, high-profile job.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-72) On May 12, 2015, he narrowly escaped injury when the train he took home [derailed and crashed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Philadelphia_train_derailment "2015 Philadelphia train derailment") in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") shortly after he debarked.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-73) In 2024, [Newark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark,_Delaware "Newark, Delaware") Train Station was renamed in his honor.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-74)

### Finances

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Finances")]

As of 2018, according to OpenSecrets.org, Carper's net worth was more than $5.7 million.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-net-worth-75)

In August 2023, [Congresstrading.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congresstrading.com "Congresstrading.com") tweeted that Carper, a senior member of the Senate Finance Committee, made an inverse Nasdaq [ETF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exchange-traded_fund "Exchange-traded fund") purchase, a [short sell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_sell "Short sell") option for investors looking to hedge against or profit from a decline in the index. The tweet questioned whether this was a conflict of interest for Carper.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Moorcraft_2023-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Carper#cite_note-Congresstrading.com_tweet_2023-08-02-77)

## Almanac

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tom_Carper&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Almanac")]

Elections are held the first Tuesday after November 1. The Governor and State Treasurer take office the third Tuesday of January. The Governor has a four-year term and the State Treasurer had a two-year term at this time. U.S. Representatives take office January 3 and have a two-year term. U.S. Senators also take office January 3, but have a six-year term.

  UNDER THE INFLUENCE: THE BINGE DRINKING EPIDEMIC ON COLLEGE CAMPUSES

                              ----------                              

                        WEDNESDAY, MAY 15, 2002

                                       U.S. Senate,
                         Committee on Governmental Affairs,
                                                    Washington, DC.
    The Committee met, pursuant to notice, at 9:35 a.m., in 
room SD-342, Dirksen Senate Office Building, Hon. Joseph I. 
Lieberman, Chairman of the Committee, presiding.
    Present: Senators Lieberman and Carper.

            OPENING STATEMENT OF CHAIRMAN LIEBERMAN

    Chairman Lieberman. The hearing will come to order. Good 
morning. Thanks to all of you for being here.
    Today we are here to talk about a very serious public 
health problem and our message is a simple but serious one, 
which is that alcohol abuse on college campuses has reached a 
point where it is far more destructive than most people realize 
and today it threatens too many of our young people. College 
students need to know that if they party to excess, they could 
die, and college administrators need to know that intervention 
is the only way to get this out-of-control behavior under 
control.
    I came to this concern, which led to this hearing today, 
from simply observing, listening, and watching what was 
happening in my home State of Connecticut. Within the last 12 
months, six college students have died in alcohol-related 
incidents. Eighty-five alcohol-related arrests were made during 
the University of Connecticut's spring weekend this year, and 
last week, Trinity College suspended one of its oldest 
fraternities.
    The numbers here are alarming. The rate of death and injury 
is extremely alarming, especially given Connecticut's 
relatively small size, but I have come to understand that this 
is not an anomaly. It is not unusual. Connecticut is, sadly, 
just a part of a nationwide trend among college students to get 
as drunk as possible as quickly as possible, often with 
devastating effects.
    Obviously, I know that many people consider drinking to be 
just another rite of passage for many college students and I 
can even remember my own college days and such behavior. But 
drinking is not the issue here. What we are concerned about is 
drinking in excess, binge drinking, drinking one's self to 
death. This type of behavior is not a harmless initiation into 
adulthood and is not a sport. It is reckless behavior, toxic 
conduct that can cut young lives short.
    We are fortunate to have with us today the Acting Director 
of the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, 
which has recently published a powerful study illustrating the 
seriousness of the problem of heavy episodic drinking on 
American college campuses. The study found that while the 
proportion of non-drinking students has actually risen, so too 
have extreme forms of drinking. The upshot is that drinking by 
college students between the ages of 18 and 24 contributes to 
1,400 deaths a year, 70,000 cases of sexual assault or rape, 
and 500,000 injuries.
    Let me repeat those numbers because they are, to me, 
stunning. Each year, college drinking contributes to 1,400 
deaths, almost half the number of lives lost in the terrorist 
attacks against us on September 11, 70,000 sexual assaults or 
rapes, and 500,000 injuries.
    Additionally, the Surgeon General has identified binge 
drinking among college students as a major public health 
problem. About 40 percent of students apparently binge drink, 
according to one study, and that is defined as five or more 
drinks in a row for men and four or more drinks for women. One 
recent survey found that 20 percent of students reported 
binging more than three times over a 2-week period.
    Most binge drinkers are freshmen. Most are men. Most attend 
schools where fraternities, sororities, or athletics dominate 
campus life, and curiously, and to me interestingly, the 
National Institute also found that most binge drinking occurs 
in the Northeast. That is, more of it occurs proportionately in 
the Northeast than any other section of the country.
    Clearly, the culture of high-risk drinking is a problem 
that touches not just a few students and their families or a 
few campuses but entire communities, and in that sense, the 
Nation.
    Edward Malloy, the President of the University of Notre 
Dame, Father Malloy, who co-chairs the National Institute on 
Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism Task Force on College Drinking, 
has said that even though ``a minority of college students 
engage in high-risk drinking, all students and their parents, 
faculty, and members of the surrounding community suffer the 
negative consequences of alcohol abuse, and that includes 
assault, vandalism, and traffic accidents.''
    So our obvious question is, what is being done about this? 
In my opinion, based on what I have learned to date, not enough 
is being done. Some colleges are actively working to revise 
their alcohol policies. Others are struggling with policy 
changes. But, frankly, from what I can see thus far, too many 
more are denying that a problem even exists.
    I paid a very encouraging visit to the University of 
Connecticut campus in Storrs on Monday, where I heard of an 
aggressive new program that is directed at this problem. And, 
there are some other colleges that are implementing similar 
programs as well. For example, the California State University 
system is a model of intervention. After the alcohol overdose 
of a freshman fraternity pledge, the California State system 
adopted a comprehensive set of policies to reduce alcohol abuse 
among students, which includes educational programs, training, 
intervention, and treatment. The California State University 
system, I think, should be commended for understanding that to 
sit on the sidelines is to await the worst, including the death 
of more students.
    More colleges and universities need to be implementing 
tougher alcohol policies and working with communities and local 
law enforcement to enforce minimum drinking age laws, to 
increase enforcement at campus events where excessive drinking 
is promoted, and to inform incoming students and their parents 
about alcohol policies and penalties.
    I do not know, as we begin this hearing, whether there is 
any appropriate legislative response from Congress or State 
legislatures to this public health problem. In the first 
instance, we are holding this hearing to educate the Committee, 
but also in that sense to educate the public and, hopefully, to 
engender action and reaction from students, from parents, from 
faculty, and from college and university administrators that 
will save lives.
    As the research shows, excessive alcohol consumption 
threatens the health and safety of students and disturbs and 
threatens the lives of those who live in communities 
surrounding the campuses. So we have got to redouble our 
efforts to bring this kind of alcohol consumption under 
control, to provide students with the tools to make more 
informed decisions so that we save the lives of as many 
students as possible.
    We have two panels of witnesses today. The first are people 
who have done research and work in the field and we are 
delighted that they are with us. Dr. Mark Goldman is the 
Director of the Alcohol and Substance Abuse Research Institute 
at the University of South Florida. Dr. Ralph Hingson is 
professor and Associate Dean of Research at the Boston 
University School of Public Health. Dr. Raynard Kington is the 
Acting Director of the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and 
Alcoholism, National Institutes of Health, U.S. Department of 
Health and Human Services.
    Dr. Kington, I would like to begin with you. We have your 
and all the other witnesses' prepared statements, for which we 
thank you. They are very well done and very helpful. We will 
enter them fully in the record and I ask that you proceed for 
approximately 5 minutes. We have a light system here which will 
let you know when you have a minute to go. If you have a little 
more than a minute, do not fear that we will close the mike 
because we want to hear you out. Anyway, thank you for being 
here and good morning. We welcome your testimony now.

 DIRECTOR, NATIONAL INSTITUTE ON ALCOHOL ABUSE AND ALCOHOLISM,

    Dr. Kington. Thank you and good morning, Mr. Chairman. My 
name is Raynard Kington. I am Acting Director of the National 
Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, also known as NIAAA, 
of the National Institutes of Health. Thank you for inviting me 
here to discuss an extremely important public health issue, 
excessive and high-risk drinking among students at our Nation's 
colleges and universities.
