# Bob Casey, Former U.S. Senator, Joins University of Scranton

Former U.S. Sen. Bob Casey will mentor students and interact with University of Scranton faculty and administration as Leahy Distinguished Fellow.

![Image 5: A man in a suit delivering a speech at a podium with the University of Scranton logo in the background.](https://news.scranton.edu/articles/2025/08/images/i-casey-announcement.jpg)

![Image 6](https://news.scranton.edu/_assets/images/icons/caption-large.svg)![Image 7](https://news.scranton.edu/_assets/images/icons/caption.svg)Former U.S. Senator Bob Casey, who served three terms in office, has returned to his hometown as a Leahy Distinguished Fellow in Public Service at The University of Scranton. Sen. Casey will maintain a consistent presence on campus, working with students, faculty and administrators in numerous areas where his expertise in public service and leadership will provide value.

Former U.S. Senator Bob Casey has joined The University of Scranton as a Leahy Distinguished Fellow in Public Service, a role that will engage the Scrantonian and three-term senator across several aspects of campus life.

Sen. Casey, drawing on his experience from 18 years in the Senate and a decade in statewide positions, will mentor students, advise on relevant initiatives and broadly contribute to University activities aligned with public service and leadership.

Speaking Tuesday at an event announcing his hire, Sen. Casey said he is excited and grateful to provide students with a “real-world perspective” on government, policy, politics and elections. He also said he hopes to instill an appreciation for and understanding of public service in all students — not just those interested in politics.

“All of us together can provide opportunities for young people to learn about public service, to be inspired to serve,” Sen. Casey said. “It doesn’t have to be public office. It doesn’t have to be in government. Even if you’re running the biggest corporation in the world, you can still work on behalf of the public in some fashion.”

Born and raised in Scranton, Sen. Casey has dedicated his life to public service. He’s won six statewide elections, serving as Pennsylvania’s Auditor General for two terms (1997-2005) and State Treasurer for one term (2005-2007) before being elected to the U.S. Senate in 2006. He remained in office until 2024-25.

“As difficult as it is and as onerous as it could be on the candidate or the public official, it is still a high calling,” Sen. Casey said. “We need the next generation — some of whom are in this room — of young people in the United States of America to choose to serve. They might choose to serve and have different points of view than I do, or other students might have. But just like the University’s Center for Ethics and Excellence in Public Service is already doing, I believe it’s critically important that young people are inspired and even taught that if you serve in public office, you have to do it ethically. You could have different points of view or a different philosophy, but everybody’s got to be ethical.”

Over the course of his 18 years in the U.S. Senate, Sen. Casey earned a reputation as an effective legislator known for his ability to work across party lines and focus on practical solutions. He authored and passed 99 pieces of legislation into law, including the Achieving a Better Life Experience (ABLE) Act, widely recognized as the most impactful piece of legislation for people with disabilities since the Americans with Disabilities Act. As chair of the Senate Special Committee on Aging and a longtime member of the Finance and HELP (Health, Education, Labor and Pension) Committees, Sen. Casey established himself as one of the leading advocates in Congress for children, workers, seniors and people with disabilities.

![Image 8: Two individuals stand at a news conference, one holding a University of Scranton T-shirt.](https://news.scranton.edu/articles/2025/08/images/casey-press4.jpg)

“I am truly delighted to welcome Senator Casey to our University,” said Rev. Joseph G. Marina, S.J., University president. “His Jesuit education has served him well for decades and I have no doubt he will continue to bring his Jesuit values to bear in this exciting, new role. I am very grateful to the Senator and the Leahys for making this new initiative possible.”

The University of Scranton is a Catholic, Jesuit institution, guided by the spiritual and intellectual legacy of St. Ignatius, whose principles inform how the University teaches and serves. These principles, including _magis_ (striving to do more and be greater) and _cura personalis_(care for each person), are familiar to Sen. Casey, who graduated from Jesuit institutions Scranton Preparatory High School and the College of the Holy Cross. He spent a year as a Jesuit volunteer, teaching and coaching in North Philadelphia, before earning a law degree from Catholic University.

“Public service is infused with Jesuit values,” Sen. Casey said. “I think we have to bring those values to the public square and try to move our society forward.”

In this part-time position, Sen. Casey will mentor and guide students interested in pursuing public service careers; advise the Center for Ethics and Excellence in Public Service on program initiatives and share expertise with regional government entities through its outreach activities; and serve as a resource for the campus and the broader community on health care, aging, ethics, government accountability and public service issues through lectures and seminars. He will also assist University administrators with government relations and resource development efforts.

The Leahy Fellow is supported by **Edward ’68, H’01** and Patricia Leahy. The longtime University benefactors are synonymous with service and achievement at The University of Scranton, which dedicated Edward R. Leahy Hall in 2015 in honor of their late son, Edward, Jr., and named the Leahy College of Health Sciences in their honor.

“I think this is a really important day — a ‘hallmark’ day, a ‘signal’ day, whatever you want to call it — in the life of this University,” Edward Leahy said. “Today, we celebrate the union of the values of a great, Jesuit University, joining with a leader with integrity who has embodied the principles of ethics in government.

“Our students, the entire University and the community at-large will have the opportunity to benefit from the programs, the advice, the discussions.”

The former Senator and his wife, Terese, reside just a few blocks from campus, having lived for the last 35 years in a house in the city’s Hill Section.

# Bob Casey, Former U.S. Senator, Joins University of Scranton

Former U.S. Sen. Bob Casey will mentor students and interact with University of Scranton faculty and administration as Leahy Distinguished Fellow.

![Image 5: A man in a suit delivering a speech at a podium with the University of Scranton logo in the background.](https://news.scranton.edu/articles/2025/08/images/i-casey-announcement.jpg)

![Image 6](https://news.scranton.edu/_assets/images/icons/caption-large.svg)![Image 7](https://news.scranton.edu/_assets/images/icons/caption.svg)Former U.S. Senator Bob Casey, who served three terms in office, has returned to his hometown as a Leahy Distinguished Fellow in Public Service at The University of Scranton. Sen. Casey will maintain a consistent presence on campus, working with students, faculty and administrators in numerous areas where his expertise in public service and leadership will provide value.

Former U.S. Senator Bob Casey has joined The University of Scranton as a Leahy Distinguished Fellow in Public Service, a role that will engage the Scrantonian and three-term senator across several aspects of campus life.

Sen. Casey, drawing on his experience from 18 years in the Senate and a decade in statewide positions, will mentor students, advise on relevant initiatives and broadly contribute to University activities aligned with public service and leadership.

Speaking Tuesday at an event announcing his hire, Sen. Casey said he is excited and grateful to provide students with a “real-world perspective” on government, policy, politics and elections. He also said he hopes to instill an appreciation for and understanding of public service in all students — not just those interested in politics.

“All of us together can provide opportunities for young people to learn about public service, to be inspired to serve,” Sen. Casey said. “It doesn’t have to be public office. It doesn’t have to be in government. Even if you’re running the biggest corporation in the world, you can still work on behalf of the public in some fashion.”

Born and raised in Scranton, Sen. Casey has dedicated his life to public service. He’s won six statewide elections, serving as Pennsylvania’s Auditor General for two terms (1997-2005) and State Treasurer for one term (2005-2007) before being elected to the U.S. Senate in 2006. He remained in office until 2024-25.

“As difficult as it is and as onerous as it could be on the candidate or the public official, it is still a high calling,” Sen. Casey said. “We need the next generation — some of whom are in this room — of young people in the United States of America to choose to serve. They might choose to serve and have different points of view than I do, or other students might have. But just like the University’s Center for Ethics and Excellence in Public Service is already doing, I believe it’s critically important that young people are inspired and even taught that if you serve in public office, you have to do it ethically. You could have different points of view or a different philosophy, but everybody’s got to be ethical.”

Over the course of his 18 years in the U.S. Senate, Sen. Casey earned a reputation as an effective legislator known for his ability to work across party lines and focus on practical solutions. He authored and passed 99 pieces of legislation into law, including the Achieving a Better Life Experience (ABLE) Act, widely recognized as the most impactful piece of legislation for people with disabilities since the Americans with Disabilities Act. As chair of the Senate Special Committee on Aging and a longtime member of the Finance and HELP (Health, Education, Labor and Pension) Committees, Sen. Casey established himself as one of the leading advocates in Congress for children, workers, seniors and people with disabilities.

![Image 8: Two individuals stand at a news conference, one holding a University of Scranton T-shirt.](https://news.scranton.edu/articles/2025/08/images/casey-press4.jpg)

“I am truly delighted to welcome Senator Casey to our University,” said Rev. Joseph G. Marina, S.J., University president. “His Jesuit education has served him well for decades and I have no doubt he will continue to bring his Jesuit values to bear in this exciting, new role. I am very grateful to the Senator and the Leahys for making this new initiative possible.”

The University of Scranton is a Catholic, Jesuit institution, guided by the spiritual and intellectual legacy of St. Ignatius, whose principles inform how the University teaches and serves. These principles, including _magis_ (striving to do more and be greater) and _cura personalis_(care for each person), are familiar to Sen. Casey, who graduated from Jesuit institutions Scranton Preparatory High School and the College of the Holy Cross. He spent a year as a Jesuit volunteer, teaching and coaching in North Philadelphia, before earning a law degree from Catholic University.

“Public service is infused with Jesuit values,” Sen. Casey said. “I think we have to bring those values to the public square and try to move our society forward.”

In this part-time position, Sen. Casey will mentor and guide students interested in pursuing public service careers; advise the Center for Ethics and Excellence in Public Service on program initiatives and share expertise with regional government entities through its outreach activities; and serve as a resource for the campus and the broader community on health care, aging, ethics, government accountability and public service issues through lectures and seminars. He will also assist University administrators with government relations and resource development efforts.

The Leahy Fellow is supported by **Edward ’68, H’01** and Patricia Leahy. The longtime University benefactors are synonymous with service and achievement at The University of Scranton, which dedicated Edward R. Leahy Hall in 2015 in honor of their late son, Edward, Jr., and named the Leahy College of Health Sciences in their honor.

“I think this is a really important day — a ‘hallmark’ day, a ‘signal’ day, whatever you want to call it — in the life of this University,” Edward Leahy said. “Today, we celebrate the union of the values of a great, Jesuit University, joining with a leader with integrity who has embodied the principles of ethics in government.

“Our students, the entire University and the community at-large will have the opportunity to benefit from the programs, the advice, the discussions.”

The former Senator and his wife, Terese, reside just a few blocks from campus, having lived for the last 35 years in a house in the city’s Hill Section.

**Robert Patrick Casey Jr.** (born April 13, 1960) is an American lawyer and politician. He served as a [U.S. Senator](https://kids.kiddle.co/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") for [Pennsylvania](https://kids.kiddle.co/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania") from 2007 to 2025. He is a member of the [Democratic Party](https://kids.kiddle.co/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)").

Born in [Scranton, Pennsylvania](https://kids.kiddle.co/Scranton,_Pennsylvania "Scranton, Pennsylvania"), Casey is the son of [Bob Casey Sr.](https://kids.kiddle.co/Bob_Casey_Sr. "Bob Casey Sr."), who was a former [governor of Pennsylvania](https://kids.kiddle.co/List_of_governors_of_Pennsylvania "List of governors of Pennsylvania"). After finishing college and law school, he worked as a lawyer in Scranton. He then started his political career as the Pennsylvania Auditor General. He was elected to this job in 1996 and held it until 2005.

In 2002, Casey ran to become the governor of Pennsylvania but lost in the Democratic primary election. After his time as auditor general ended, he was elected [State Treasurer](https://kids.kiddle.co/Treasurer_of_Pennsylvania "Treasurer of Pennsylvania") in 2004. In 2006, Casey ran for the U.S. Senate and won against the Republican Senator, [Rick Santorum](https://kids.kiddle.co/Rick_Santorum "Rick Santorum"). Casey was reelected in 2012 and 2018. In 2024, he lost his reelection bid to Republican David McCormick by a very small difference.

## Early Life and School

Bob Casey Jr. was born in [Scranton, Pennsylvania](https://kids.kiddle.co/Scranton,_Pennsylvania "Scranton, Pennsylvania"), on April 13, 1960. He was one of eight children of Ellen and [Bob Casey Sr.](https://kids.kiddle.co/Bob_Casey_Sr. "Bob Casey Sr."), who became the 42nd [governor of Pennsylvania](https://kids.kiddle.co/List_of_governors_of_Pennsylvania "List of governors of Pennsylvania"). His family has Irish roots.

Casey played basketball at Scranton Preparatory School and graduated in 1978. He earned his first degree from the [College of the Holy Cross](https://kids.kiddle.co/College_of_the_Holy_Cross "College of the Holy Cross") in 1982. Later, he received a law degree from The Catholic University of America in 1988. Before law school, Casey volunteered with the Jesuit Volunteer Corps. He spent a year teaching 5th grade and coaching basketball in [Francisville, Philadelphia](https://kids.kiddle.co/Francisville,_Philadelphia "Francisville, Philadelphia"). He worked as a lawyer in Scranton from 1988 until 1996.

## Starting in Politics

### Working as State Auditor

Casey first ran for Pennsylvania State Auditor General in 1996. The Auditor General is like a chief accountant for the state. This person checks how state money is spent to make sure it's used correctly. Casey won the Democratic nomination and then the general election. He was reelected in 2000 and served two terms, from 1997 to 2005.

### Running for Governor in 2002

In 2002, Casey tried to become the [governor of Pennsylvania](https://kids.kiddle.co/List_of_governors_of_Pennsylvania "List of governors of Pennsylvania"), following in his father's footsteps. He ran against former [Philadelphia Mayor](https://kids.kiddle.co/Mayor_of_Philadelphia "Mayor of Philadelphia")[Ed Rendell](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ed_Rendell "Ed Rendell") in the Democratic primary election. The primary was very expensive. Rendell won the nomination by winning in Philadelphia and its nearby areas. After the primary, Casey supported Rendell, who then won the general election.

### Serving as State Treasurer

In 2004, Casey was elected [State Treasurer](https://kids.kiddle.co/Treasurer_of_Pennsylvania "Treasurer of Pennsylvania"). The Treasurer manages the state's money and investments. He served in this job from 2005 to 2007.

## U.S. Senate (2007–2025)

### Senate Elections

#### 2006 Election

[![Image 4: Bob Casey Swearing-In](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/c/c1/Bob_Casey_Swearing-In.jpg/300px-Bob_Casey_Swearing-In.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Bob_Casey_Swearing-In.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Bob_Casey_Swearing-In.jpg "Enlarge")

 Casey being sworn into the [Senate](https://kids.kiddle.co/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") by Vice President [Dick Cheney](https://kids.kiddle.co/Dick_Cheney "Dick Cheney") in January 2007

In 2005, leaders of the Democratic Party asked Casey to run for the U.S. Senate. He decided to run against the Republican Senator, [Rick Santorum](https://kids.kiddle.co/Rick_Santorum "Rick Santorum"). Casey started his campaign on March 5, 2005. This was his fifth time running for a statewide office in nine years.

Casey quickly received support from [Governor](https://kids.kiddle.co/List_of_governors_of_Pennsylvania "List of governors of Pennsylvania")[Ed Rendell](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ed_Rendell "Ed Rendell"). Some people thought Casey's views on social issues were too conservative for many Pennsylvania Democrats. However, Casey believed his views would help him gain support from different groups. He won the Democratic primary election in May with 85% of the votes.

On election night, Casey won the Senate race with 59% of the votes, while Santorum received 41%. Casey's victory margin was the largest for a Democrat running for Senate in Pennsylvania.

#### 2012 Election

[![Image 5: 2012 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania results map by county](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/5/54/2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania_results_map_by_county.svg/300px-2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania_results_map_by_county.svg.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania_results_map_by_county.svg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania_results_map_by_county.svg "Enlarge")

 Results of the 2012 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania by county

Casey ran for reelection in 2012. He easily won the Democratic primary. In the general election, he faced Republican [Tom Smith](https://kids.kiddle.co/Tom_Smith_(Pennsylvania_politician) "Tom Smith (Pennsylvania politician)"). Casey won the election on November 6, with 53.7% of the votes. This made him the first Democrat from Pennsylvania to be elected to a second Senate term since 1962.

#### 2018 Election

Casey won his third Senate term in 2018. He defeated Republican [Lou Barletta](https://kids.kiddle.co/Lou_Barletta "Lou Barletta") with 55.7% of the votes. This victory made Casey the first Democrat in Pennsylvania history to win six statewide elections.

#### 2024 Election

Casey ran for a fourth Senate term in 2024. He lost to Republican David McCormick by a very small margin of 0.22%. This was the closest Senate race in 2024. After the election, Casey said he lost because he didn't get enough votes in the Philadelphia area and lost support in rural parts of the state.

### Time in the Senate

[![Image 6: Governor Wolf Joins Ag Industry to Celebrate PA Farm Bill (48538912662)](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/3/31/Governor_Wolf_Joins_Ag_Industry_to_Celebrate_PA_Farm_Bill_%2848538912662%29.jpg/300px-Governor_Wolf_Joins_Ag_Industry_to_Celebrate_PA_Farm_Bill_%2848538912662%29.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Governor_Wolf_Joins_Ag_Industry_to_Celebrate_PA_Farm_Bill_(48538912662).jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Governor_Wolf_Joins_Ag_Industry_to_Celebrate_PA_Farm_Bill_(48538912662).jpg "Enlarge")

 Casey speaks at the 2019 Agriculture Progress Days

Casey supported [Barack Obama](https://kids.kiddle.co/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") in the 2008 Democratic presidential primaries. His early support for Obama gave him good access to the White House.

Casey was known as a moderate senator. However, after [Donald Trump](https://kids.kiddle.co/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") became president in 2017, Casey became more vocal in his opposition to many of Trump's actions. This new approach was seen as a strategy for his 2018 reelection campaign.

### Committee Work

[![Image 7: Senator Bob Casey Committee of Aging (cropped)](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/6/6c/Senator_Bob_Casey_Committee_of_Aging_%28cropped%29.jpg/300px-Senator_Bob_Casey_Committee_of_Aging_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Committee_of_Aging_(cropped).jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Committee_of_Aging_(cropped).jpg "Enlarge")

 Casey [chairing](https://kids.kiddle.co/Chair_(officer) "Chair (officer)") the Senate Committee on Aging

Senators work in different committees to focus on specific topics. Casey was part of several important committees:

*   Committee on Finance: This committee deals with taxes, trade, and social security.
*   [Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions](https://kids.kiddle.co/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Health,_Education,_Labor_and_Pensions "United States Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions"): This committee focuses on health care, education, and workplace safety. He was the Chairman of the Subcommittee on Children and Families.
*   Select Committee on Intelligence: This committee oversees U.S. intelligence agencies.
*   Special Committee on Aging: This committee focuses on issues affecting older Americans. Casey was the Chairman of this committee.

### Group Memberships

Casey was also a member of the Afterschool Caucuses. These groups bring together senators who are interested in specific issues.

## Political Views

### Economy and Jobs

[![Image 8: Senator Bob Casey Helicopter Factory](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/c/c9/Senator_Bob_Casey_Helicopter_Factory.jpg/300px-Senator_Bob_Casey_Helicopter_Factory.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Helicopter_Factory.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Helicopter_Factory.jpg "Enlarge")

 Casey at the Piasecki factory highlighting manufacturing jobs that his work has helped create in [Pennsylvania](https://kids.kiddle.co/Coatesville,_Pennsylvania "Coatesville, Pennsylvania")

In 2014, Casey released a report about income inequality in Pennsylvania. He urged Congress to raise the [minimum wage](https://kids.kiddle.co/Minimum_wage "Minimum wage") and increase funding for early education. He believed the U.S. should do more to stop other countries from selling steel at very low prices, which hurts American steel companies.

In 2023, Casey introduced bills about how companies use Artificial Intelligence (AI) and watch their workers. One bill, the No Robot Bosses Act, would stop employers from using only AI to make decisions about hiring or firing.

In 2024, Casey introduced the Shrinkflation Protection Act. This bill would prevent companies from making products smaller without also lowering the price. He also introduced the Price Gouging Prevention Act, which would ban "grossly excessive price increases."

### Education

[![Image 9: Senator Bob Casey Bernville Training Facility](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/6/6c/Senator_Bob_Casey_Bernville_Training_Facility.jpg/300px-Senator_Bob_Casey_Bernville_Training_Facility.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Bernville_Training_Facility.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Bernville_Training_Facility.jpg "Enlarge")

 Casey at the new Operating Engineers Local 542 training facility in [Bernville](https://kids.kiddle.co/Bernville,_Pennsylvania "Bernville, Pennsylvania")

As a candidate in 2004, Casey was against school vouchers. He supported using state money to make sure families had access to good, affordable early childhood education programs.

### Environment

Casey believed that [global warming](https://kids.kiddle.co/Global_warming "Global warming") was a danger. He accused his Republican opponent, Rick Santorum, of not recognizing this threat.

### Foreign Policy

Casey worked with other senators to urge the [European Union](https://kids.kiddle.co/European_Union "European Union") to call [Hezbollah](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hezbollah "Hezbollah") a terrorist group. He also introduced a bill to punish countries that allow terrorist financing. Casey voted for a law to stop the U.S. from being a market for stolen ancient items from Syria.

He spoke out against the violence against the [Rohingya Muslim](https://kids.kiddle.co/Rohingya_people "Rohingya people") minority in [Myanmar](https://kids.kiddle.co/Myanmar "Myanmar"). In 2019, Casey and other senators wrote to President Trump. They argued that helping Central American countries financially could reduce migration to the U.S. by improving conditions there.

In 2024, Casey voted against a proposal to apply human rights rules to U.S. military aid to Israel. The proposal did not pass.

### Government Spending and Taxes

[![Image 10: Senator Bob Casey Invest in America](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/1/1b/Senator_Bob_Casey_Invest_in_America.jpg/300px-Senator_Bob_Casey_Invest_in_America.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Invest_in_America.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Invest_in_America.jpg "Enlarge")

 Casey highlights the success of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021

In 2012, Casey introduced a bill to extend a payroll tax cut and give [tax credits](https://kids.kiddle.co/Tax_credit "Tax credit") to businesses that created jobs.

In 2016, Casey joined other senators who wanted to extend benefits for retired coal workers. He said he would vote against a spending bill if these benefits were not continued.

Casey voted against the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. He said it mostly helped very wealthy people.

### Gun Policy

In 2012, Casey changed his views on gun control. He became a strong supporter of gun control laws. He supported banning assault weapons and improving background checks for gun purchases.

He said that after the Sandy Hook tragedy, his wife and daughter asked him how he would vote on gun issues. This made him think deeply about it. He decided it was unacceptable that the [National Rifle Association](https://kids.kiddle.co/National_Rifle_Association "National Rifle Association") (NRA) opposed all new gun laws. He then supported common-sense gun measures.

### Healthcare

[![Image 11: Senator Bob Casey Preexisting Conditions](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/b/b2/Senator_Bob_Casey_Preexisting_Conditions.jpg/300px-Senator_Bob_Casey_Preexisting_Conditions.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Preexisting_Conditions.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Preexisting_Conditions.jpg "Enlarge")

 Casey pushes to preserve the [Affordable Care Act](https://kids.kiddle.co/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act") which the [Trump administration](https://kids.kiddle.co/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump") is attempting to repeal, 2019

Casey supported President Obama's health reform law, the [Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act](https://kids.kiddle.co/Patient_Protection_and_Affordable_Care_Act "Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act").

In 2019, Casey helped introduce a bill called the American Miners Act. This bill aimed to protect health care and pension benefits for retired coal miners.

When asked about "Medicare for All," Casey said he supported "universal coverage." This means he wants everyone to have health insurance.

### Housing

In 2019, Casey and other senators wrote a letter supporting the Section 4 Capacity Building program. This program helps local community groups improve their neighborhoods. They were disappointed that President Trump's budget planned to cut this program.

### Immigration Laws

Casey supported a bill in 2007 that would have created a way for undocumented people in the U.S. to become legal citizens. He also supported continuing federal funds for "sanctuary cities." These are cities that limit their cooperation with national immigration enforcement.

In 2017, Casey protested President Trump's travel ban at the Philadelphia International Airport. He also asked the Homeland Security Secretary to stop the detention of children and mothers at a facility in Pennsylvania. He spoke out against the deportation of a 5-year-old boy and his mother from Honduras who were seeking asylum.

In 2019, Casey and other senators asked for an investigation into federal contractors. They were concerned that some contractors were not providing proper care for children in their facilities.

### Judicial Nominees

Casey supported the confirmation of [John Roberts](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Roberts "John Roberts") in 2005 and [Samuel Alito](https://kids.kiddle.co/Samuel_Alito "Samuel Alito") in 2006 to the [Supreme Court of the United States](https://kids.kiddle.co/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States").

He voted to confirm [Sonia Sotomayor](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sonia_Sotomayor "Sonia Sotomayor") in 2009 and [Elena Kagan](https://kids.kiddle.co/Elena_Kagan "Elena Kagan") in 2010 to the Supreme Court.

Casey voted against confirming [Neil Gorsuch](https://kids.kiddle.co/Neil_Gorsuch "Neil Gorsuch") in 2017, [Brett Kavanaugh](https://kids.kiddle.co/Brett_Kavanaugh "Brett Kavanaugh") in 2018, and [Amy Coney Barrett](https://kids.kiddle.co/Amy_Coney_Barrett "Amy Coney Barrett") in 2020 to the Supreme Court. He had concerns about their judicial philosophies and past opinions.

### LGBT Rights

Casey voted for the law that ended "Don't Ask, Don't Tell" in 2010. This policy had prevented openly gay people from serving in the military. He supported civil unions for same-sex couples for a long time. In 2013, he announced his support for same-sex marriage. He also supports same-sex couples adopting children.

In 2019, Casey and other senators asked the [United States Secretary of State](https://kids.kiddle.co/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State") why the State Department did not issue a statement for [Pride Month](https://kids.kiddle.co/Gay_pride#LGBT_Pride_Month "Gay pride"). They also asked why the special envoy position for LGBTI issues was empty. They believed this signaled that the U.S. was not prioritizing LGBTI rights in its foreign policy.

## Personal Life

Bob Casey Jr. and his wife, Terese, got married in 1985. They have four children.

In 2023, Casey received treatment for prostate cancer.

His brother, Patrick Casey, is a lobbyist. A lobbyist tries to influence lawmakers on behalf of a group or company.

Casey is Catholic.

**Robert Patrick Casey Jr.** (born April 13, 1960) is an American lawyer and politician. He served as a [U.S. Senator](https://kids.kiddle.co/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") for [Pennsylvania](https://kids.kiddle.co/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania") from 2007 to 2025. He is a member of the [Democratic Party](https://kids.kiddle.co/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)").

Born in [Scranton, Pennsylvania](https://kids.kiddle.co/Scranton,_Pennsylvania "Scranton, Pennsylvania"), Casey is the son of [Bob Casey Sr.](https://kids.kiddle.co/Bob_Casey_Sr. "Bob Casey Sr."), who was a former [governor of Pennsylvania](https://kids.kiddle.co/List_of_governors_of_Pennsylvania "List of governors of Pennsylvania"). After finishing college and law school, he worked as a lawyer in Scranton. He then started his political career as the Pennsylvania Auditor General. He was elected to this job in 1996 and held it until 2005.

In 2002, Casey ran to become the governor of Pennsylvania but lost in the Democratic primary election. After his time as auditor general ended, he was elected [State Treasurer](https://kids.kiddle.co/Treasurer_of_Pennsylvania "Treasurer of Pennsylvania") in 2004. In 2006, Casey ran for the U.S. Senate and won against the Republican Senator, [Rick Santorum](https://kids.kiddle.co/Rick_Santorum "Rick Santorum"). Casey was reelected in 2012 and 2018. In 2024, he lost his reelection bid to Republican David McCormick by a very small difference.

## Early Life and School

Bob Casey Jr. was born in [Scranton, Pennsylvania](https://kids.kiddle.co/Scranton,_Pennsylvania "Scranton, Pennsylvania"), on April 13, 1960. He was one of eight children of Ellen and [Bob Casey Sr.](https://kids.kiddle.co/Bob_Casey_Sr. "Bob Casey Sr."), who became the 42nd [governor of Pennsylvania](https://kids.kiddle.co/List_of_governors_of_Pennsylvania "List of governors of Pennsylvania"). His family has Irish roots.

Casey played basketball at Scranton Preparatory School and graduated in 1978. He earned his first degree from the [College of the Holy Cross](https://kids.kiddle.co/College_of_the_Holy_Cross "College of the Holy Cross") in 1982. Later, he received a law degree from The Catholic University of America in 1988. Before law school, Casey volunteered with the Jesuit Volunteer Corps. He spent a year teaching 5th grade and coaching basketball in [Francisville, Philadelphia](https://kids.kiddle.co/Francisville,_Philadelphia "Francisville, Philadelphia"). He worked as a lawyer in Scranton from 1988 until 1996.

## Starting in Politics

### Working as State Auditor

Casey first ran for Pennsylvania State Auditor General in 1996. The Auditor General is like a chief accountant for the state. This person checks how state money is spent to make sure it's used correctly. Casey won the Democratic nomination and then the general election. He was reelected in 2000 and served two terms, from 1997 to 2005.

### Running for Governor in 2002

In 2002, Casey tried to become the [governor of Pennsylvania](https://kids.kiddle.co/List_of_governors_of_Pennsylvania "List of governors of Pennsylvania"), following in his father's footsteps. He ran against former [Philadelphia Mayor](https://kids.kiddle.co/Mayor_of_Philadelphia "Mayor of Philadelphia")[Ed Rendell](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ed_Rendell "Ed Rendell") in the Democratic primary election. The primary was very expensive. Rendell won the nomination by winning in Philadelphia and its nearby areas. After the primary, Casey supported Rendell, who then won the general election.

### Serving as State Treasurer

In 2004, Casey was elected [State Treasurer](https://kids.kiddle.co/Treasurer_of_Pennsylvania "Treasurer of Pennsylvania"). The Treasurer manages the state's money and investments. He served in this job from 2005 to 2007.

## U.S. Senate (2007–2025)

### Senate Elections

#### 2006 Election

[![Image 4: Bob Casey Swearing-In](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/c/c1/Bob_Casey_Swearing-In.jpg/300px-Bob_Casey_Swearing-In.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Bob_Casey_Swearing-In.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Bob_Casey_Swearing-In.jpg "Enlarge")

 Casey being sworn into the [Senate](https://kids.kiddle.co/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") by Vice President [Dick Cheney](https://kids.kiddle.co/Dick_Cheney "Dick Cheney") in January 2007

In 2005, leaders of the Democratic Party asked Casey to run for the U.S. Senate. He decided to run against the Republican Senator, [Rick Santorum](https://kids.kiddle.co/Rick_Santorum "Rick Santorum"). Casey started his campaign on March 5, 2005. This was his fifth time running for a statewide office in nine years.

Casey quickly received support from [Governor](https://kids.kiddle.co/List_of_governors_of_Pennsylvania "List of governors of Pennsylvania")[Ed Rendell](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ed_Rendell "Ed Rendell"). Some people thought Casey's views on social issues were too conservative for many Pennsylvania Democrats. However, Casey believed his views would help him gain support from different groups. He won the Democratic primary election in May with 85% of the votes.

On election night, Casey won the Senate race with 59% of the votes, while Santorum received 41%. Casey's victory margin was the largest for a Democrat running for Senate in Pennsylvania.

#### 2012 Election

[![Image 5: 2012 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania results map by county](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/5/54/2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania_results_map_by_county.svg/300px-2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania_results_map_by_county.svg.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania_results_map_by_county.svg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania_results_map_by_county.svg "Enlarge")

 Results of the 2012 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania by county

Casey ran for reelection in 2012. He easily won the Democratic primary. In the general election, he faced Republican [Tom Smith](https://kids.kiddle.co/Tom_Smith_(Pennsylvania_politician) "Tom Smith (Pennsylvania politician)"). Casey won the election on November 6, with 53.7% of the votes. This made him the first Democrat from Pennsylvania to be elected to a second Senate term since 1962.

#### 2018 Election

Casey won his third Senate term in 2018. He defeated Republican [Lou Barletta](https://kids.kiddle.co/Lou_Barletta "Lou Barletta") with 55.7% of the votes. This victory made Casey the first Democrat in Pennsylvania history to win six statewide elections.

#### 2024 Election

Casey ran for a fourth Senate term in 2024. He lost to Republican David McCormick by a very small margin of 0.22%. This was the closest Senate race in 2024. After the election, Casey said he lost because he didn't get enough votes in the Philadelphia area and lost support in rural parts of the state.

### Time in the Senate

[![Image 6: Governor Wolf Joins Ag Industry to Celebrate PA Farm Bill (48538912662)](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/3/31/Governor_Wolf_Joins_Ag_Industry_to_Celebrate_PA_Farm_Bill_%2848538912662%29.jpg/300px-Governor_Wolf_Joins_Ag_Industry_to_Celebrate_PA_Farm_Bill_%2848538912662%29.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Governor_Wolf_Joins_Ag_Industry_to_Celebrate_PA_Farm_Bill_(48538912662).jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Governor_Wolf_Joins_Ag_Industry_to_Celebrate_PA_Farm_Bill_(48538912662).jpg "Enlarge")

 Casey speaks at the 2019 Agriculture Progress Days

Casey supported [Barack Obama](https://kids.kiddle.co/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") in the 2008 Democratic presidential primaries. His early support for Obama gave him good access to the White House.

Casey was known as a moderate senator. However, after [Donald Trump](https://kids.kiddle.co/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") became president in 2017, Casey became more vocal in his opposition to many of Trump's actions. This new approach was seen as a strategy for his 2018 reelection campaign.

### Committee Work

[![Image 7: Senator Bob Casey Committee of Aging (cropped)](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/6/6c/Senator_Bob_Casey_Committee_of_Aging_%28cropped%29.jpg/300px-Senator_Bob_Casey_Committee_of_Aging_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Committee_of_Aging_(cropped).jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Committee_of_Aging_(cropped).jpg "Enlarge")

 Casey [chairing](https://kids.kiddle.co/Chair_(officer) "Chair (officer)") the Senate Committee on Aging

Senators work in different committees to focus on specific topics. Casey was part of several important committees:

*   Committee on Finance: This committee deals with taxes, trade, and social security.
*   [Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions](https://kids.kiddle.co/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Health,_Education,_Labor_and_Pensions "United States Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions"): This committee focuses on health care, education, and workplace safety. He was the Chairman of the Subcommittee on Children and Families.
*   Select Committee on Intelligence: This committee oversees U.S. intelligence agencies.
*   Special Committee on Aging: This committee focuses on issues affecting older Americans. Casey was the Chairman of this committee.

### Group Memberships

Casey was also a member of the Afterschool Caucuses. These groups bring together senators who are interested in specific issues.

## Political Views

### Economy and Jobs

[![Image 8: Senator Bob Casey Helicopter Factory](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/c/c9/Senator_Bob_Casey_Helicopter_Factory.jpg/300px-Senator_Bob_Casey_Helicopter_Factory.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Helicopter_Factory.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Helicopter_Factory.jpg "Enlarge")

 Casey at the Piasecki factory highlighting manufacturing jobs that his work has helped create in [Pennsylvania](https://kids.kiddle.co/Coatesville,_Pennsylvania "Coatesville, Pennsylvania")

In 2014, Casey released a report about income inequality in Pennsylvania. He urged Congress to raise the [minimum wage](https://kids.kiddle.co/Minimum_wage "Minimum wage") and increase funding for early education. He believed the U.S. should do more to stop other countries from selling steel at very low prices, which hurts American steel companies.

In 2023, Casey introduced bills about how companies use Artificial Intelligence (AI) and watch their workers. One bill, the No Robot Bosses Act, would stop employers from using only AI to make decisions about hiring or firing.

In 2024, Casey introduced the Shrinkflation Protection Act. This bill would prevent companies from making products smaller without also lowering the price. He also introduced the Price Gouging Prevention Act, which would ban "grossly excessive price increases."

### Education

[![Image 9: Senator Bob Casey Bernville Training Facility](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/6/6c/Senator_Bob_Casey_Bernville_Training_Facility.jpg/300px-Senator_Bob_Casey_Bernville_Training_Facility.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Bernville_Training_Facility.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Bernville_Training_Facility.jpg "Enlarge")

 Casey at the new Operating Engineers Local 542 training facility in [Bernville](https://kids.kiddle.co/Bernville,_Pennsylvania "Bernville, Pennsylvania")

As a candidate in 2004, Casey was against school vouchers. He supported using state money to make sure families had access to good, affordable early childhood education programs.

### Environment

Casey believed that [global warming](https://kids.kiddle.co/Global_warming "Global warming") was a danger. He accused his Republican opponent, Rick Santorum, of not recognizing this threat.

### Foreign Policy

Casey worked with other senators to urge the [European Union](https://kids.kiddle.co/European_Union "European Union") to call [Hezbollah](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hezbollah "Hezbollah") a terrorist group. He also introduced a bill to punish countries that allow terrorist financing. Casey voted for a law to stop the U.S. from being a market for stolen ancient items from Syria.

He spoke out against the violence against the [Rohingya Muslim](https://kids.kiddle.co/Rohingya_people "Rohingya people") minority in [Myanmar](https://kids.kiddle.co/Myanmar "Myanmar"). In 2019, Casey and other senators wrote to President Trump. They argued that helping Central American countries financially could reduce migration to the U.S. by improving conditions there.

In 2024, Casey voted against a proposal to apply human rights rules to U.S. military aid to Israel. The proposal did not pass.

### Government Spending and Taxes

[![Image 10: Senator Bob Casey Invest in America](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/1/1b/Senator_Bob_Casey_Invest_in_America.jpg/300px-Senator_Bob_Casey_Invest_in_America.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Invest_in_America.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Invest_in_America.jpg "Enlarge")

 Casey highlights the success of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021

In 2012, Casey introduced a bill to extend a payroll tax cut and give [tax credits](https://kids.kiddle.co/Tax_credit "Tax credit") to businesses that created jobs.

In 2016, Casey joined other senators who wanted to extend benefits for retired coal workers. He said he would vote against a spending bill if these benefits were not continued.

Casey voted against the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. He said it mostly helped very wealthy people.

### Gun Policy

In 2012, Casey changed his views on gun control. He became a strong supporter of gun control laws. He supported banning assault weapons and improving background checks for gun purchases.

He said that after the Sandy Hook tragedy, his wife and daughter asked him how he would vote on gun issues. This made him think deeply about it. He decided it was unacceptable that the [National Rifle Association](https://kids.kiddle.co/National_Rifle_Association "National Rifle Association") (NRA) opposed all new gun laws. He then supported common-sense gun measures.

### Healthcare

[![Image 11: Senator Bob Casey Preexisting Conditions](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/b/b2/Senator_Bob_Casey_Preexisting_Conditions.jpg/300px-Senator_Bob_Casey_Preexisting_Conditions.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Preexisting_Conditions.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Senator_Bob_Casey_Preexisting_Conditions.jpg "Enlarge")

 Casey pushes to preserve the [Affordable Care Act](https://kids.kiddle.co/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act") which the [Trump administration](https://kids.kiddle.co/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump") is attempting to repeal, 2019

Casey supported President Obama's health reform law, the [Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act](https://kids.kiddle.co/Patient_Protection_and_Affordable_Care_Act "Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act").

In 2019, Casey helped introduce a bill called the American Miners Act. This bill aimed to protect health care and pension benefits for retired coal miners.

When asked about "Medicare for All," Casey said he supported "universal coverage." This means he wants everyone to have health insurance.

### Housing

In 2019, Casey and other senators wrote a letter supporting the Section 4 Capacity Building program. This program helps local community groups improve their neighborhoods. They were disappointed that President Trump's budget planned to cut this program.

### Immigration Laws

Casey supported a bill in 2007 that would have created a way for undocumented people in the U.S. to become legal citizens. He also supported continuing federal funds for "sanctuary cities." These are cities that limit their cooperation with national immigration enforcement.

In 2017, Casey protested President Trump's travel ban at the Philadelphia International Airport. He also asked the Homeland Security Secretary to stop the detention of children and mothers at a facility in Pennsylvania. He spoke out against the deportation of a 5-year-old boy and his mother from Honduras who were seeking asylum.

In 2019, Casey and other senators asked for an investigation into federal contractors. They were concerned that some contractors were not providing proper care for children in their facilities.

### Judicial Nominees

Casey supported the confirmation of [John Roberts](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Roberts "John Roberts") in 2005 and [Samuel Alito](https://kids.kiddle.co/Samuel_Alito "Samuel Alito") in 2006 to the [Supreme Court of the United States](https://kids.kiddle.co/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States").

He voted to confirm [Sonia Sotomayor](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sonia_Sotomayor "Sonia Sotomayor") in 2009 and [Elena Kagan](https://kids.kiddle.co/Elena_Kagan "Elena Kagan") in 2010 to the Supreme Court.

Casey voted against confirming [Neil Gorsuch](https://kids.kiddle.co/Neil_Gorsuch "Neil Gorsuch") in 2017, [Brett Kavanaugh](https://kids.kiddle.co/Brett_Kavanaugh "Brett Kavanaugh") in 2018, and [Amy Coney Barrett](https://kids.kiddle.co/Amy_Coney_Barrett "Amy Coney Barrett") in 2020 to the Supreme Court. He had concerns about their judicial philosophies and past opinions.

### LGBT Rights

Casey voted for the law that ended "Don't Ask, Don't Tell" in 2010. This policy had prevented openly gay people from serving in the military. He supported civil unions for same-sex couples for a long time. In 2013, he announced his support for same-sex marriage. He also supports same-sex couples adopting children.

In 2019, Casey and other senators asked the [United States Secretary of State](https://kids.kiddle.co/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State") why the State Department did not issue a statement for [Pride Month](https://kids.kiddle.co/Gay_pride#LGBT_Pride_Month "Gay pride"). They also asked why the special envoy position for LGBTI issues was empty. They believed this signaled that the U.S. was not prioritizing LGBTI rights in its foreign policy.

## Personal Life

Bob Casey Jr. and his wife, Terese, got married in 1985. They have four children.

In 2023, Casey received treatment for prostate cancer.

His brother, Patrick Casey, is a lobbyist. A lobbyist tries to influence lawmakers on behalf of a group or company.

Casey is Catholic.

**Robert Patrick Casey Jr.** (born April 13, 1960) is an American lawyer and politician who served from 2007 to 2025 as a [United States senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") from [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"). He is a member of the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)").

Born in [Scranton, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scranton,_Pennsylvania "Scranton, Pennsylvania"), Casey is the son of [Bob Casey Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Sr. "Bob Casey Sr."), a former [governor of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Pennsylvania "Governor of Pennsylvania"). After graduating from the [College of the Holy Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_the_Holy_Cross "College of the Holy Cross") and the [Catholic University of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_University_of_America_Columbus_School_of_Law "Catholic University of America Columbus School of Law"), he practiced law in Scranton before beginning his political career as [Pennsylvania Auditor General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Auditor_General "Pennsylvania Auditor General"), a position he was elected to in 1996 and held until 2005.

In [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Pennsylvania_gubernatorial_election "2002 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election"), Casey ran for governor of Pennsylvania, but lost the Democratic primary to [Ed Rendell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Rendell "Ed Rendell"). After being term-limited out of his position as auditor general, Casey was elected [treasurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Treasurer "Pennsylvania Treasurer") in [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Pennsylvania_State_Treasurer_election "2004 Pennsylvania State Treasurer election"). In [2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2006 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania"), Casey ran for the U.S. Senate and defeated the [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") incumbent, [Rick Santorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Santorum "Rick Santorum"). Casey was reelected in [2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2012 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania") and in [2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2018 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania"). In [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2024 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania"), he narrowly lost reelection to Republican nominee [David McCormick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_McCormick "Dave McCormick") by a 0.22% margin.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-1)

## Early life and education

Robert Patrick Casey Jr. was born in [Scranton, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scranton,_Pennsylvania "Scranton, Pennsylvania"), on April 13, 1960, one of eight children of Ellen (née Harding) and [Bob Casey Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Sr. "Bob Casey Sr."), the 42nd [governor of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Pennsylvania "Governor of Pennsylvania"). He is of Irish descent.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-2)

Casey played basketball at [Scranton Preparatory School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scranton_Preparatory_School "Scranton Preparatory School"), from which he graduated in 1978. He graduated from the [College of the Holy Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_the_Holy_Cross "College of the Holy Cross") in [Worcester, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester,_Massachusetts "Worcester, Massachusetts"), with a [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") in 1982, then earned a [Juris Doctor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor") from the [Columbus School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_School_of_Law "Columbus School of Law") at [The Catholic University of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Catholic_University_of_America "The Catholic University of America") in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), in 1988.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-3) Between college and law school, Casey served as a member of the [Jesuit Volunteer Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit_Volunteer_Corps "Jesuit Volunteer Corps") and spent a year teaching 5th grade and coaching basketball at the Gesu School in [Francisville, Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisville,_Philadelphia "Francisville, Philadelphia").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Brit-4) He practiced law in Scranton from 1988 until 1996.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Brit-4)

## Early political career

### State auditor

Casey ran for [Pennsylvania State Auditor General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_Auditor_General "Pennsylvania State Auditor General") in [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Pennsylvania_Auditor_General_election "1996 Pennsylvania Auditor General election"), winning the Democratic nomination.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-5) He won the general election and was reelected in [2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Pennsylvania_Auditor_General_election "2000 Pennsylvania Auditor General election"), serving two terms, from 1997 to 2005.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-6)

In a 2002 [PoliticsPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PoliticsPA "PoliticsPA") feature story designating politicians with [yearbook superlatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yearbook "Yearbook"), Casey was named "Most Likely to Succeed".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-yearbook-7)

### 2002 gubernatorial election

Main article: [2002 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Pennsylvania_gubernatorial_election "2002 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election")

Casey attempted to follow in his father's footsteps by running for [governor of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Pennsylvania "List of governors of Pennsylvania"). He faced former [Philadelphia Mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Philadelphia "Mayor of Philadelphia")[Ed Rendell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Rendell "Ed Rendell") in the Democratic [primary election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partisan_primary "Partisan primary"). Rendell had run for governor and lost to Casey's father in [1986](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_Pennsylvania_gubernatorial_election "1986 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election"). The Pennsylvania Democratic Party supported Casey, whom it saw as more electable than Rendell due to his popularity among Democrats statewide, strong support from unions, and name recognition. He chose [Jack Wagner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Wagner_(politician) "Jack Wagner (politician)") as his running mate.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-8)

In a bitter primary, classified as the then-most expensive in Pennsylvania's history,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-9) Rendell won the nomination by winning only 10 out of 67 counties: [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_County,_Pennsylvania "Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania") and [its suburbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_metropolitan_area "Philadelphia metropolitan area") ([Bucks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucks_County,_Pennsylvania "Bucks County, Pennsylvania"), [Chester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chester_County,_Pennsylvania "Chester County, Pennsylvania"), [Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_County,_Pennsylvania "Montgomery County, Pennsylvania"), and [Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_County,_Pennsylvania "Delaware County, Pennsylvania")), its [Lehigh Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehigh_Valley "Lehigh Valley")[exurbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exurb "Exurb") ([Berks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berks_County,_Pennsylvania "Berks County, Pennsylvania"), [Lehigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehigh_County,_Pennsylvania "Lehigh County, Pennsylvania"), and [Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northampton_County,_Pennsylvania "Northampton County, Pennsylvania")), [Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_County,_Pennsylvania "Lancaster County, Pennsylvania"), and [Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_County,_Pennsylvania "Centre County, Pennsylvania"), the home of [Penn State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_University "Pennsylvania State University").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-10) Casey endorsed Rendell after the primary and Rendell won the general election.

### State treasurer

In [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Pennsylvania_State_Treasurer_election "2004 Pennsylvania State Treasurer election"), Casey, who was term limited as auditor general, was elected [State Treasurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_Treasurer "Pennsylvania State Treasurer"). He served in this position from 2005 to 2007.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-11)

## U.S. Senate (2007–2025)

### Elections

#### 2006

Main article: [2006 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2006 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Bob_Casey_Swearing-In.jpg/250px-Bob_Casey_Swearing-In.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bob_Casey_Swearing-In.jpg)

Casey being sworn into the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") by Vice President [Dick Cheney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Cheney "Dick Cheney") in January 2007

In 2005, Casey received calls from U.S. Senators [Chuck Schumer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Schumer "Chuck Schumer"), the chair of the [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Senatorial_Campaign_Committee "Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee"), and [Harry Reid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Reid "Harry Reid"), the [Senate minority leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_Minority_Leader "Senate Minority Leader"). Both asked him to run for U.S. Senate in the [2006 U.S. Senate election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2006 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania") against Republican incumbent [Rick Santorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Santorum "Rick Santorum"). On March 5, 2005, Casey launched his campaign for the Democratic nomination. His run for the Senate was his fifth statewide campaign in nine years.

Casey was almost immediately endorsed by [Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Pennsylvania "Governor of Pennsylvania")[Ed Rendell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Rendell "Ed Rendell"), his primary election opponent from [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_gubernatorial_elections,_2002 "United States gubernatorial elections, 2002").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-12) He was endorsed by two Democrats who had been mentioned as possible U.S. Senate nominees: former [Congressman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives")[Joe Hoeffel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Hoeffel "Joe Hoeffel"), who had run against Pennsylvania's other Senator, [Arlen Specter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlen_Specter "Arlen Specter"), in 2004, and former [State Treasurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Treasurer "Pennsylvania Treasurer")[Barbara Hafer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Hafer "Barbara Hafer"), whom many in the [abortion rights movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion-rights_movements "Abortion-rights movements") had attempted to convince to run against Casey in the Democratic primary.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Casey's more [socially conservative views](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Democrat "Conservative Democrat") led to two challenges in the Democratic primary. His two challengers, college professor Chuck Pennacchio and pension lawyer Alan Sandals, argued that Casey's views on abortion and other social issues were too conservative for most [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania") Democrats. Casey challenged this, arguing his opinions gave him cross-party appeal. He defeated both challengers in the May 16 primary with 85% of the vote.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-14)

On election night, Casey won the race with 59% of the vote to Santorum's 41%. Casey's 17.4-point victory margin was the highest ever for a Democrat running for Senate in Pennsylvania.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-15) It was also the largest for a challenger to any incumbent Senator since [James Abdnor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Abdnor "James Abdnor") unseated [George McGovern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_McGovern "George McGovern") by 18.8 points in [1980](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_election_in_South_Dakota,_1980 "United States Senate election in South Dakota, 1980").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-16)

#### 2012

Main article: [2012 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2012 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania")

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania_results_map_by_county.svg/250px-2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania_results_map_by_county.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania_results_map_by_county.svg)

Results of the [2012 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2012 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania") by county

Casey sought reelection in 2012.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-ppg01-18) His prospects were uncertain. Observers noted that as the election approached, Casey, an early supporter of Obama, had "started to oppose the president outright or developed more nuanced responses to events that differentiate him from Mr. Obama. Analysts say Mr. Casey wants to put some distance between himself and a president whose job approval ratings in Pennsylvania are poor".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-19) In December 2011, it was reported that the [AFL–CIO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL%E2%80%93CIO "AFL–CIO") would spend "over $170,000" on pro-Casey TV ads.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-20)

Casey easily defeated challenger Joseph Vodvarka in the Democratic primary, and faced the Republican nominee, former coal company owner [Tom Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Smith_(Pennsylvania_politician) "Tom Smith (Pennsylvania politician)"), in the general election. He defeated Smith on November 6, 53.7% to 44.6%, making him the first Democrat elected to a second term in the Senate from Pennsylvania since [Joseph S. Clark Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_S._Clark_Jr. "Joseph S. Clark Jr.") in 1962.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-senate-21)

#### 2018

Main article: [2018 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2018 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania")

Casey defeated the Republican nominee, U.S. Congressman and former Hazelton mayor [Lou Barletta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Barletta "Lou Barletta"), 55.7% to 42.6%. The victory made Casey the first Democrat to be elected to a third term in state history, as well as the first to win six statewide elections.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-24)

#### 2024

Main article: [2024 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2024 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania")

Casey ran for a fourth Senate term in 2024 and lost to Republican nominee [David McCormick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_McCormick "David McCormick") by 0.22%, in the closest Senate race of the 2024 cycle.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-25) In an interview after the election, Casey attributed his defeat to not winning enough votes in the [Philadelphia metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_metropolitan_area "Philadelphia metropolitan area"), while losing ground in the state's rural areas.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-26)

### Tenure

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Governor_Wolf_Joins_Ag_Industry_to_Celebrate_PA_Farm_Bill_%2848538912662%29.jpg/250px-Governor_Wolf_Joins_Ag_Industry_to_Celebrate_PA_Farm_Bill_%2848538912662%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Governor_Wolf_Joins_Ag_Industry_to_Celebrate_PA_Farm_Bill_(48538912662).jpg)

Casey speaks at the 2019 Agriculture Progress Days

Casey endorsed [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") in the [Democratic presidential primaries of 2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States)_presidential_primaries,_2008 "Democratic Party (United States) presidential primaries, 2008").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-27) The _Pennsylvania Report_ said he "struck gold" by endorsing Obama early in the [primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Democratic_primary,_2008 "Pennsylvania Democratic primary, 2008"), a move that gave him "inside access to the halls of the White House".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-pareport2009-28) Casey campaigned across Pennsylvania in support of Obama's candidacy in the months leading up to the primary in that state; they bowled together at Pleasant Valley Lanes in [Altoona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altoona,_Pennsylvania "Altoona, Pennsylvania").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-29)

Casey has been called an "even-keeled moderate, not only in tone but in policy", but after [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") became president in 2017, Casey developed a "new, saltier social media prowess". His outspoken opposition to many of Trump's actions prompted one local media outlet to describe his new strategy before his 2018 reelection campaign as "Oppose Trump every chance he gets".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Owens_Cassie-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-31)

In February 2018, while speaking to [John Catsimatidis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Catsimatidis "John Catsimatidis") on New York radio station [WNYM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WNYM "WNYM"), Casey issued a warning to [special counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_counsel "Special counsel")[Robert Mueller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mueller "Robert Mueller") not to deliver a report on his findings in the [Russian interference in the 2016 United States elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_interference_in_the_2016_United_States_elections "Russian interference in the 2016 United States elections") investigation too near to the [2018 midterm elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_midterm_elections "2018 midterm elections"). While saying he could not "make any assumptions about where the Mueller investigation is going", he said he "would recommend Mueller not release a report on his findings near the midterms" because it would "distract from elections or cause people to question the election's integrity".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-32)

## Political positions

### Economic issues

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Senator_Bob_Casey_Helicopter_Factory.jpg/250px-Senator_Bob_Casey_Helicopter_Factory.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Senator_Bob_Casey_Helicopter_Factory.jpg)

Casey at the [Piasecki factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piasecki_Aircraft "Piasecki Aircraft") highlighting manufacturing jobs that his work has helped create in [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coatesville,_Pennsylvania "Coatesville, Pennsylvania")

In 2014, Casey released a report on [income inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_inequality "Income inequality") in Pennsylvania and urged Congress to raise the [minimum wage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_wage "Minimum wage"), extend unemployment insurance, and increase funding for early education.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-38) He has said he believes that the United States has not exhausted its options to stop foreign countries from flooding the country with steel supplies, and that he wanted the Trump administration to defend [nuclear power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power "Nuclear power") in Pennsylvania.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-39)

### Gun policy

Casey discusses [gun safety policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_politics_in_the_United_States "Gun politics in the United States") in 2022

In 2016, _[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Post "The Washington Post")_ reported that "'pro-gun' Bob Casey" had become "an evangelist for gun control laws". After the [Sandy Hook school massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandy_Hook_Elementary_School_shooting "Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting") in 2012, he had "completely flipped his views" on several gun issues, largely as a result of having been "accosted" by his wife and daughter. "Casey has since embraced every major proposal to counter gun violence", the _Post_ reported, "including a renewed ban on assault weapons and enhanced background checks before gun purchases." In the wake of the [Orlando Pulse massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando_nightclub_shooting "Orlando nightclub shooting"), he unveiled the [Hate Crimes Prevention Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hate_Crimes_Prevention_Act "Hate Crimes Prevention Act"), which would have prevented people convicted of [hate crimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hate_crimes "Hate crimes") from buying guns. He said he had never really thought about the gun issue until Sandy Hook, "coasting along with Pennsylvania's traditional pro-gun views in a state where the [National Rifle Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rifle_Association "National Rifle Association") has held sway for decades". After Sandy Hook, he "found it unacceptable that the NRA opposed any new laws".[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-64)

[_Philadelphia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_(magazine) "Philadelphia (magazine)") magazine ran an article the same year about Casey's "profound about-face on gun control", noting that it had taken place in "a matter of days" and that Casey "was the first to introduce gun control legislation after the massacre in Orlando". Casey said his switch had been a result of "thinking of the enormity of it, what happened to those children, which was indescribably horrific, and then having my wife and daughter say to me, 'You're going to vote on this at some point. How are you going to vote?'" He said: "I had to ask myself that question, because normally I would stay in my lane. There's only two lanes on this. It's the NRA lane or the voting for commonsense gun measures lane. So I decided whether I was going to stay in the old lane, in which I had traveled a long time but really had never been challenged or had to cast a real big vote."[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-65)
