#### Abortion

Casey formerly identified as pro-life[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Politico2-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-72) and expressed support for overturning _[Roe v. Wade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roe\_v.\_Wade "Roe v. Wade")._[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-73) In 2005, he opposed funding [embryonic stem cell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embryonic_stem_cell "Embryonic stem cell") research.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-74) In 2006, he supported the [Democrats for Life of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democrats_for_Life_of_America "Democrats for Life of America")'s [Pregnant Women Support Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pregnant_Women_Support_Act "Pregnant Women Support Act"),[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-75) which sought to reduce abortion by supporting women experiencing unplanned pregnancies. Casey has voted against barring HHS grants to organizations that provide abortion services, where such services may often not be central to the organization's chief purpose.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-76)

In 2010, during a debate on the [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act"), Casey was heckled for his handling of the abortion provisions in the bill and for not taking an uncompromising anti-abortion stance. He was the primary sponsor of an amendment to prevent government funds from being used for abortion services, but when he tried to organize a compromise that appealed to the party's lone Senate holdout, [Ben Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Nelson "Ben Nelson"), he angered some religious groups.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-78)

In 2011, Casey voted against defunding [Planned Parenthood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_Parenthood "Planned Parenthood") and cutting funding for contraception, and for cloture for the nomination of [Goodwin Liu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodwin_Liu "Goodwin Liu"), earning him a 100% rating from NARAL.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-79) The same year, Casey said he supported over-the-counter sale of the morning-after pill for [emergency contraception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_contraception "Emergency contraception").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-80) In the 2012 election, [NARAL Pro-Choice America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NARAL_Pro-Choice_America "NARAL Pro-Choice America")'s election guide endorsed Casey.

In 2015 and 2018, Casey joined two other Democratic senators, [Joe Manchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Manchin "Joe Manchin") and [Joe Donnelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Donnelly "Joe Donnelly"), in voting for bills that would ban abortion after 20 weeks of pregnancy.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-81)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-82) In 2017, he voted for legislation that would have overturned the [Mexico City Policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City_Policy "Mexico City Policy"), which prohibits foreign aid for organizations that provide or promote abortion.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-nationalreview.com-84) His vote prompted anti-abortion activists to question his commitment to their cause.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-nationalreview.com-84) The [National Right to Life Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Right_to_Life_Committee "National Right to Life Committee") criticized Casey for his 2017 vote against the confirmation of [Neil Gorsuch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Gorsuch "Neil Gorsuch") to the Supreme Court of the United States.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-85)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Politico2-71)

In 2018, _Politico_ wrote:

> After a decade in the Senate, Casey has become an increasingly reliable vote in support of abortion rights—scoring as high as 100 percent on [NARAL Pro-Choice America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NARAL "NARAL")'s vote tally in 2016 and 2017 ... although his 2018 rating is sure to be lower.

_Politico_ acknowledged that scorecards "are an imperfect calculation of a lawmaker's position", adding that Casey asserted that he had voted anti-abortion on 13 of the 15 abortion-related measures during his career.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Politico2-71) According to _Politico_, "Like conservative anti-abortion groups, [Casey] opposes the _Roe_ decision and opposes the taxpayer funding of the [abortion] procedure. But like progressive abortion rights organizations, he supports Obamacare, access to contraception through programs such as Title X and funding for Planned Parenthood."[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Politico2-71) Casey considers contraception a tool to reduce the demand for abortions. He has called on greater funding for access to contraceptives, specifically supporting Planned Parenthood's efforts to make them more accessible.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Politico2-71)

In 2022, Casey fully reversed his [anti-abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-abortion "Anti-abortion") position and said he supported legislation to codify national abortion rights.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-86)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-88) He and 45 other senators voted to allow debate to continue on the [Women's Health Protection Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Health_Protection_Act "Women's Health Protection Act") in a roll-call vote on February 28.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-89) He voted for the measure again on May 11 in the wake of the leak of the _[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobbs\_v.\_Jackson\_Women's\_Health\_Organization "Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization")_ decision. He said that if the bill passed [cloture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloture "Cloture"), he would still vote for it.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-90)

Casey took part in a [Philadelphia International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_International_Airport "Philadelphia International Airport") protest against President Trump's January [2017 travel ban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_13769 "Executive Order 13769").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Owens_Cassie-30) Leaving a black-tie event to join the protest, he tweeted: "I won't stand by as the promise of America is diminished."[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-95) In May, Casey, nine other senators, and 13 U.S. representatives requested in a letter to the [Homeland Security Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeland_Security_Secretary "Homeland Security Secretary") that they stop the detention of four children and their mothers at the [Berks County Residential Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._Don_Hutto_Residential_Center "T. Don Hutto Residential Center"). Many of the families had been detained there without legal recourse for more than a year and a half. Casey also personally took to social media with impassioned appeals to the White House on behalf of a Honduran 5-year-old and his 25-year-old mother being held at the facility who were facing deportation. They had fled violence and death threats and sought asylum in the U.S. in 2015, but failed their [credible fear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credible_fear "Credible fear") interview. Attorneys had been appealing their case, and the legal team was in the middle of the process of applying for [Special Immigrant Juvenile Status](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Immigrant_Juvenile_Status "Special Immigrant Juvenile Status") for the child when they were awakened at 3:30AM on May 3 by [Immigration and Customs Enforcement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration_and_Customs_Enforcement "Immigration and Customs Enforcement") and put on a plane to Honduras. "This child and his mother deserved better from this Administration. They got the absolute worst", Casey said.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-96)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-97)

In 2019, Casey and six other Democratic senators led by [Brian Schatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Schatz "Brian Schatz") sent letters to the Government Accountability Office and the suspension and debarment official and inspector general at the Department of Health and Human Services citing recent reports that showed "significant evidence that some federal contractors and grantees have not provided adequate accommodations for children in line with legal and contractual requirements" and urging officials to determine whether federal contractors and grantees were in violation of contractual obligations or federal regulations and should thus face financial consequences.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-98)

### Judicial nominees

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/2016_March_22_Senator_Bob_Casey_and_Merrick_Garland_01.jpg/250px-2016_March_22_Senator_Bob_Casey_and_Merrick_Garland_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2016_March_22_Senator_Bob_Casey_and_Merrick_Garland_01.jpg)

Casey meets with [Merrick Garland whose Supreme Court nomination in 2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland_Supreme_Court_nomination "Merrick Garland Supreme Court nomination") the Senate Republicans blocked

Casey expressed support for the confirmation of both [John Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_G._Roberts "John G. Roberts") in 2005[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-99) and [Samuel Alito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Alito "Samuel Alito") in 2006[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-100) to the [Supreme Court of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States"); both were believed to be in favor of overturning [Roe v. Wade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roe_v._Wade "Roe v. Wade").

He voted to confirm both [Sonia Sotomayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonia_Sotomayor "Sonia Sotomayor") in 2009[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-101) and [Elena Kagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elena_Kagan "Elena Kagan") in 2010 to the [Supreme Court of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States").[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-102)

Casey voted against confirming [Neil Gorsuch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Gorsuch "Neil Gorsuch") in 2017 to the Supreme Court, citing "real concerns" about Gorsuch's "rigid and restrictive" judicial philosophy and some of his past opinions on issues relating to the health and safety of workers and the rights of those with disabilities.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-103) He also voted against the [confirmation of Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brett_Kavanaugh_Supreme_Court_nomination "Brett Kavanaugh Supreme Court nomination") in 2018.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-104) He voted against the [confirmation of Amy Coney Barrett to the Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amy_Coney_Barrett_Supreme_Court_nomination "Amy Coney Barrett Supreme Court nomination") in 2020.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-105)

### LGBT rights

Casey voted for the [Don't Ask, Don't Tell Repeal Act of 2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Ask,_Don't_Tell_Repeal_Act_of_2010 "Don't Ask, Don't Tell Repeal Act of 2010").[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-106)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-107) A longtime supporter of civil unions, Casey stated his support for same-sex marriage in 2013.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-108)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-109) He also supports the adoption of children by same-sex couples.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-autogenerated1-43)

Casey was one of 18 senators to sign a letter in 2019 to [United States Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State")[Mike Pompeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pompeo "Mike Pompeo") requesting an explanation of a State Department decision not to issue an official statement that year commemorating [Pride Month](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay_pride#LGBT_Pride_Month "Gay pride") or issue the annual cable outlining activities for embassies commemorating Pride Month. They also asked why the LGBTI special envoy position had remained vacant and wrote, "preventing the official flying of rainbow flags and limiting public messages celebrating Pride Month signals to the international community that the United States is abandoning the advancement of LGBTI rights as a foreign policy priority."[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-110)

## Personal life

Casey and his wife, Terese, were married in 1985, and have four children.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-111)

In 2023, Casey was treated for [prostate cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prostate_cancer "Prostate cancer").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-112)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-113)

His brother Patrick Casey is a [lobbyist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lobbying_in_the_United_States "Lobbying in the United States") who has reported lobbying the U.S. Senate on a number of issues.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-114)

Casey is Catholic.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-115)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-116)

In 2025, Casey joined the [University of Scranton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Scranton "University of Scranton") as a public service advisor.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-117)

**Robert Patrick Casey Jr.** (born April 13, 1960) is an American lawyer and politician who served from 2007 to 2025 as a [United States senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") from [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"). He is a member of the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)").

Born in [Scranton, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scranton,_Pennsylvania "Scranton, Pennsylvania"), Casey is the son of [Bob Casey Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Sr. "Bob Casey Sr."), a former [governor of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Pennsylvania "Governor of Pennsylvania"). After graduating from the [College of the Holy Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_the_Holy_Cross "College of the Holy Cross") and the [Catholic University of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_University_of_America_Columbus_School_of_Law "Catholic University of America Columbus School of Law"), he practiced law in Scranton before beginning his political career as [Pennsylvania Auditor General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Auditor_General "Pennsylvania Auditor General"), a position he was elected to in 1996 and held until 2005.

In [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Pennsylvania_gubernatorial_election "2002 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election"), Casey ran for governor of Pennsylvania, but lost the Democratic primary to [Ed Rendell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Rendell "Ed Rendell"). After being term-limited out of his position as auditor general, Casey was elected [treasurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Treasurer "Pennsylvania Treasurer") in [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Pennsylvania_State_Treasurer_election "2004 Pennsylvania State Treasurer election"). In [2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2006 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania"), Casey ran for the U.S. Senate and defeated the [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") incumbent, [Rick Santorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Santorum "Rick Santorum"). Casey was reelected in [2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2012 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania") and in [2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2018 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania"). In [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2024 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania"), he narrowly lost reelection to Republican nominee [David McCormick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_McCormick "Dave McCormick") by a 0.22% margin.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-1)

## Early life and education

Robert Patrick Casey Jr. was born in [Scranton, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scranton,_Pennsylvania "Scranton, Pennsylvania"), on April 13, 1960, one of eight children of Ellen (née Harding) and [Bob Casey Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Sr. "Bob Casey Sr."), the 42nd [governor of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Pennsylvania "Governor of Pennsylvania"). He is of Irish descent.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-2)

Casey played basketball at [Scranton Preparatory School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scranton_Preparatory_School "Scranton Preparatory School"), from which he graduated in 1978. He graduated from the [College of the Holy Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_the_Holy_Cross "College of the Holy Cross") in [Worcester, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester,_Massachusetts "Worcester, Massachusetts"), with a [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") in 1982, then earned a [Juris Doctor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor") from the [Columbus School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_School_of_Law "Columbus School of Law") at [The Catholic University of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Catholic_University_of_America "The Catholic University of America") in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), in 1988.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-3) Between college and law school, Casey served as a member of the [Jesuit Volunteer Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit_Volunteer_Corps "Jesuit Volunteer Corps") and spent a year teaching 5th grade and coaching basketball at the Gesu School in [Francisville, Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisville,_Philadelphia "Francisville, Philadelphia").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Brit-4) He practiced law in Scranton from 1988 until 1996.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Brit-4)

## Early political career

### State auditor

Casey ran for [Pennsylvania State Auditor General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_Auditor_General "Pennsylvania State Auditor General") in [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Pennsylvania_Auditor_General_election "1996 Pennsylvania Auditor General election"), winning the Democratic nomination.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-5) He won the general election and was reelected in [2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Pennsylvania_Auditor_General_election "2000 Pennsylvania Auditor General election"), serving two terms, from 1997 to 2005.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-6)

In a 2002 [PoliticsPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PoliticsPA "PoliticsPA") feature story designating politicians with [yearbook superlatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yearbook "Yearbook"), Casey was named "Most Likely to Succeed".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-yearbook-7)

### 2002 gubernatorial election

Main article: [2002 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Pennsylvania_gubernatorial_election "2002 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election")

Casey attempted to follow in his father's footsteps by running for [governor of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Pennsylvania "List of governors of Pennsylvania"). He faced former [Philadelphia Mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Philadelphia "Mayor of Philadelphia")[Ed Rendell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Rendell "Ed Rendell") in the Democratic [primary election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partisan_primary "Partisan primary"). Rendell had run for governor and lost to Casey's father in [1986](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_Pennsylvania_gubernatorial_election "1986 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election"). The Pennsylvania Democratic Party supported Casey, whom it saw as more electable than Rendell due to his popularity among Democrats statewide, strong support from unions, and name recognition. He chose [Jack Wagner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Wagner_(politician) "Jack Wagner (politician)") as his running mate.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-8)

In a bitter primary, classified as the then-most expensive in Pennsylvania's history,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-9) Rendell won the nomination by winning only 10 out of 67 counties: [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_County,_Pennsylvania "Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania") and [its suburbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_metropolitan_area "Philadelphia metropolitan area") ([Bucks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucks_County,_Pennsylvania "Bucks County, Pennsylvania"), [Chester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chester_County,_Pennsylvania "Chester County, Pennsylvania"), [Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_County,_Pennsylvania "Montgomery County, Pennsylvania"), and [Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_County,_Pennsylvania "Delaware County, Pennsylvania")), its [Lehigh Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehigh_Valley "Lehigh Valley")[exurbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exurb "Exurb") ([Berks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berks_County,_Pennsylvania "Berks County, Pennsylvania"), [Lehigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehigh_County,_Pennsylvania "Lehigh County, Pennsylvania"), and [Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northampton_County,_Pennsylvania "Northampton County, Pennsylvania")), [Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_County,_Pennsylvania "Lancaster County, Pennsylvania"), and [Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_County,_Pennsylvania "Centre County, Pennsylvania"), the home of [Penn State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_University "Pennsylvania State University").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-10) Casey endorsed Rendell after the primary and Rendell won the general election.

### State treasurer

In [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Pennsylvania_State_Treasurer_election "2004 Pennsylvania State Treasurer election"), Casey, who was term limited as auditor general, was elected [State Treasurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_Treasurer "Pennsylvania State Treasurer"). He served in this position from 2005 to 2007.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-11)

## U.S. Senate (2007–2025)

### Elections

#### 2006

Main article: [2006 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2006 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Bob_Casey_Swearing-In.jpg/250px-Bob_Casey_Swearing-In.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bob_Casey_Swearing-In.jpg)

Casey being sworn into the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") by Vice President [Dick Cheney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Cheney "Dick Cheney") in January 2007

In 2005, Casey received calls from U.S. Senators [Chuck Schumer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Schumer "Chuck Schumer"), the chair of the [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Senatorial_Campaign_Committee "Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee"), and [Harry Reid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Reid "Harry Reid"), the [Senate minority leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_Minority_Leader "Senate Minority Leader"). Both asked him to run for U.S. Senate in the [2006 U.S. Senate election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2006 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania") against Republican incumbent [Rick Santorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Santorum "Rick Santorum"). On March 5, 2005, Casey launched his campaign for the Democratic nomination. His run for the Senate was his fifth statewide campaign in nine years.

Casey was almost immediately endorsed by [Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Pennsylvania "Governor of Pennsylvania")[Ed Rendell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Rendell "Ed Rendell"), his primary election opponent from [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_gubernatorial_elections,_2002 "United States gubernatorial elections, 2002").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-12) He was endorsed by two Democrats who had been mentioned as possible U.S. Senate nominees: former [Congressman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives")[Joe Hoeffel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Hoeffel "Joe Hoeffel"), who had run against Pennsylvania's other Senator, [Arlen Specter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlen_Specter "Arlen Specter"), in 2004, and former [State Treasurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Treasurer "Pennsylvania Treasurer")[Barbara Hafer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Hafer "Barbara Hafer"), whom many in the [abortion rights movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion-rights_movements "Abortion-rights movements") had attempted to convince to run against Casey in the Democratic primary.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Casey's more [socially conservative views](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Democrat "Conservative Democrat") led to two challenges in the Democratic primary. His two challengers, college professor Chuck Pennacchio and pension lawyer Alan Sandals, argued that Casey's views on abortion and other social issues were too conservative for most [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania") Democrats. Casey challenged this, arguing his opinions gave him cross-party appeal. He defeated both challengers in the May 16 primary with 85% of the vote.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-14)

On election night, Casey won the race with 59% of the vote to Santorum's 41%. Casey's 17.4-point victory margin was the highest ever for a Democrat running for Senate in Pennsylvania.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-15) It was also the largest for a challenger to any incumbent Senator since [James Abdnor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Abdnor "James Abdnor") unseated [George McGovern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_McGovern "George McGovern") by 18.8 points in [1980](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_election_in_South_Dakota,_1980 "United States Senate election in South Dakota, 1980").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-16)

#### 2012

Main article: [2012 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2012 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania")

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania_results_map_by_county.svg/250px-2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania_results_map_by_county.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania_results_map_by_county.svg)

Results of the [2012 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2012 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania") by county

Casey sought reelection in 2012.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-ppg01-18) His prospects were uncertain. Observers noted that as the election approached, Casey, an early supporter of Obama, had "started to oppose the president outright or developed more nuanced responses to events that differentiate him from Mr. Obama. Analysts say Mr. Casey wants to put some distance between himself and a president whose job approval ratings in Pennsylvania are poor".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-19) In December 2011, it was reported that the [AFL–CIO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL%E2%80%93CIO "AFL–CIO") would spend "over $170,000" on pro-Casey TV ads.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-20)

Casey easily defeated challenger Joseph Vodvarka in the Democratic primary, and faced the Republican nominee, former coal company owner [Tom Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Smith_(Pennsylvania_politician) "Tom Smith (Pennsylvania politician)"), in the general election. He defeated Smith on November 6, 53.7% to 44.6%, making him the first Democrat elected to a second term in the Senate from Pennsylvania since [Joseph S. Clark Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_S._Clark_Jr. "Joseph S. Clark Jr.") in 1962.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-senate-21)

#### 2018

Main article: [2018 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2018 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania")

Casey defeated the Republican nominee, U.S. Congressman and former Hazelton mayor [Lou Barletta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Barletta "Lou Barletta"), 55.7% to 42.6%. The victory made Casey the first Democrat to be elected to a third term in state history, as well as the first to win six statewide elections.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-24)

#### 2024

Main article: [2024 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_Senate_election_in_Pennsylvania "2024 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania")

Casey ran for a fourth Senate term in 2024 and lost to Republican nominee [David McCormick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_McCormick "David McCormick") by 0.22%, in the closest Senate race of the 2024 cycle.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-25) In an interview after the election, Casey attributed his defeat to not winning enough votes in the [Philadelphia metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_metropolitan_area "Philadelphia metropolitan area"), while losing ground in the state's rural areas.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-26)

Casey endorsed [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") in the [Democratic presidential primaries of 2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States)_presidential_primaries,_2008 "Democratic Party (United States) presidential primaries, 2008").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-27) The _Pennsylvania Report_ said he "struck gold" by endorsing Obama early in the [primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Democratic_primary,_2008 "Pennsylvania Democratic primary, 2008"), a move that gave him "inside access to the halls of the White House".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-pareport2009-28) Casey campaigned across Pennsylvania in support of Obama's candidacy in the months leading up to the primary in that state; they bowled together at Pleasant Valley Lanes in [Altoona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altoona,_Pennsylvania "Altoona, Pennsylvania").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-29)

Casey has been called an "even-keeled moderate, not only in tone but in policy", but after [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") became president in 2017, Casey developed a "new, saltier social media prowess". His outspoken opposition to many of Trump's actions prompted one local media outlet to describe his new strategy before his 2018 reelection campaign as "Oppose Trump every chance he gets".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Owens_Cassie-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-31)

In February 2018, while speaking to [John Catsimatidis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Catsimatidis "John Catsimatidis") on New York radio station [WNYM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WNYM "WNYM"), Casey issued a warning to [special counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_counsel "Special counsel")[Robert Mueller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mueller "Robert Mueller") not to deliver a report on his findings in the [Russian interference in the 2016 United States elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_interference_in_the_2016_United_States_elections "Russian interference in the 2016 United States elections") investigation too near to the [2018 midterm elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_midterm_elections "2018 midterm elections"). While saying he could not "make any assumptions about where the Mueller investigation is going", he said he "would recommend Mueller not release a report on his findings near the midterms" because it would "distract from elections or cause people to question the election's integrity".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-32)

## Political positions

### Economic issues

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Senator_Bob_Casey_Helicopter_Factory.jpg/250px-Senator_Bob_Casey_Helicopter_Factory.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Senator_Bob_Casey_Helicopter_Factory.jpg)

Casey at the [Piasecki factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piasecki_Aircraft "Piasecki Aircraft") highlighting manufacturing jobs that his work has helped create in [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coatesville,_Pennsylvania "Coatesville, Pennsylvania")

In 2014, Casey released a report on [income inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_inequality "Income inequality") in Pennsylvania and urged Congress to raise the [minimum wage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_wage "Minimum wage"), extend unemployment insurance, and increase funding for early education.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-38) He has said he believes that the United States has not exhausted its options to stop foreign countries from flooding the country with steel supplies, and that he wanted the Trump administration to defend [nuclear power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power "Nuclear power") in Pennsylvania.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-39)

In 2017, Casey was one of eight Democratic senators to sign a letter to President Trump noting government-subsidized Chinese steel had been placed into the American market in recent years below cost and had hurt the domestic steel industry and the iron ore industry that fed it, calling on Trump to raise the steel issue with [President of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_China "President of China")[Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") in his meeting with him.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-40)

In 2023, Casey introduced two bills focused on workplace AI and worker surveillance, including the No Robot Bosses Act, which prohibits employers from solely using an automated decision system to make employment-related decisions.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-41)

In 2024, Casey introduced the Shrinkflation Protection Act, which would prevent companies from selling smaller sizes of product without lowering prices, and the Price Gouging Prevention Act, which would create a federal ban on "grossly excessive price increases".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-42)

### Foreign policy

Along with over 70 other senators, Casey wrote to urge the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") to designate [Hezbollah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hezbollah "Hezbollah") as a terrorist organization.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-53) He introduced the Stop Terrorist Operational Resources and Money (STORM) Act of 2016, which punishes countries that accept terrorist financing by their citizens or within their borders. Casey voted for the [Protect and Preserve International Cultural Property Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protect_and_Preserve_International_Cultural_Property_Act "Protect and Preserve International Cultural Property Act"), which was designed to ensure that the U.S. is not a market for [antiquities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiquities "Antiquities") looted from Syria and was signed into law by Obama.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-56)

Casey condemned the [genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017%E2%80%93present_Rohingya_genocide_in_Myanmar "2017–present Rohingya genocide in Myanmar") of the [Rohingya Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohingya_people "Rohingya people") minority in [Myanmar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myanmar "Myanmar") and called for a stronger response to it.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-57)

Casey was one of 34 senators to sign a letter in 2019 to President Trump encouraging him "to listen to members of your own Administration and reverse a decision that will damage our national security and aggravate conditions inside Central America", asserting that Trump had "consistently expressed a flawed understanding of U.S. foreign assistance" since becoming president and that he was "personally undermining efforts to promote U.S. national security and economic prosperity" by preventing the use of Fiscal Year 2018 national security funding. The senators argued that foreign assistance to Central American countries created less migration to the U.S. by helping to improve conditions in those countries.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-58)

Casey voted against a resolution in 2024 proposed by Senator [Bernie Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders") to apply the [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_violations_against_Palestinians_by_Israel "Human rights violations against Palestinians by Israel") provisions of the [Foreign Assistance Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Assistance_Act "Foreign Assistance Act") to [U.S. aid to Israel's military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel%E2%80%93United_States_military_relations "Israel–United States military relations"). The proposal was defeated, 72 to 11.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-59)

### Gun policy

[Video 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/59/Senator_Bob_Casey_Gun_Safety.webm?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

Casey discusses [gun safety policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_politics_in_the_United_States "Gun politics in the United States") in 2022

In 2016, _[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Post "The Washington Post")_ reported that "'pro-gun' Bob Casey" had become "an evangelist for gun control laws". After the [Sandy Hook school massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandy_Hook_Elementary_School_shooting "Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting") in 2012, he had "completely flipped his views" on several gun issues, largely as a result of having been "accosted" by his wife and daughter. "Casey has since embraced every major proposal to counter gun violence", the _Post_ reported, "including a renewed ban on assault weapons and enhanced background checks before gun purchases." In the wake of the [Orlando Pulse massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando_nightclub_shooting "Orlando nightclub shooting"), he unveiled the [Hate Crimes Prevention Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hate_Crimes_Prevention_Act "Hate Crimes Prevention Act"), which would have prevented people convicted of [hate crimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hate_crimes "Hate crimes") from buying guns. He said he had never really thought about the gun issue until Sandy Hook, "coasting along with Pennsylvania's traditional pro-gun views in a state where the [National Rifle Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rifle_Association "National Rifle Association") has held sway for decades". After Sandy Hook, he "found it unacceptable that the NRA opposed any new laws".[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-64)

[_Philadelphia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_(magazine) "Philadelphia (magazine)") magazine ran an article the same year about Casey's "profound about-face on gun control", noting that it had taken place in "a matter of days" and that Casey "was the first to introduce gun control legislation after the massacre in Orlando". Casey said his switch had been a result of "thinking of the enormity of it, what happened to those children, which was indescribably horrific, and then having my wife and daughter say to me, 'You're going to vote on this at some point. How are you going to vote?'" He said: "I had to ask myself that question, because normally I would stay in my lane. There's only two lanes on this. It's the NRA lane or the voting for commonsense gun measures lane. So I decided whether I was going to stay in the old lane, in which I had traveled a long time but really had never been challenged or had to cast a real big vote."[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-65)

### Healthcare

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/Senator_Bob_Casey_Preexisting_Conditions.jpg/250px-Senator_Bob_Casey_Preexisting_Conditions.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Senator_Bob_Casey_Preexisting_Conditions.jpg)

Casey pushes to preserve the [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act") which the [Trump administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump") is attempting to repeal, 2019

Casey supported President Obama's health reform legislation; he voted for the [Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patient_Protection_and_Affordable_Care_Act "Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act") in 2009,[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-66) and for the [Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_Care_and_Education_Reconciliation_Act_of_2010 "Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-67)

Casey was one of six Democratic senators to introduce the American Miners Act of 2019, a bill that would amend the [Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_Mining_Control_and_Reclamation_Act_of_1977 "Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977") to swap funds in excess of the amounts needed to meet existing obligations under the Abandoned Mine Land fund to the 1974 Pension Plan as part of an effort to prevent its insolvency as a result of coal company bankruptcies and the 2008 financial crisis. It also increased the [Black Lung Disability Trust Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Lung_Benefits_Act_of_1972#Black_Lung_Disability_Trust_Fund "Black Lung Benefits Act of 1972") tax and ensured that miners affected by the 2018 coal company bankruptcies would not lose their health care.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-68)

Amid discussions to prevent a [government shutdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_shutdowns_in_the_United_States "Government shutdowns in the United States") in September 2019, Casey was one of six Democratic senators to sign a letter to congressional leadership advocating the passage of legislation that would permanently fund health care and pension benefits for retired coal miners as "families in Virginia, West Virginia, Wyoming, Alabama, Colorado, North Dakota and New Mexico" would start to receive notifications of health care termination by the end of the following month.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-70)

#### Abortion

Casey formerly identified as pro-life[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Politico2-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-72) and expressed support for overturning _[Roe v. Wade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roe\_v.\_Wade "Roe v. Wade")._[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-73) In 2005, he opposed funding [embryonic stem cell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embryonic_stem_cell "Embryonic stem cell") research.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-74) In 2006, he supported the [Democrats for Life of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democrats_for_Life_of_America "Democrats for Life of America")'s [Pregnant Women Support Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pregnant_Women_Support_Act "Pregnant Women Support Act"),[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-75) which sought to reduce abortion by supporting women experiencing unplanned pregnancies. Casey has voted against barring HHS grants to organizations that provide abortion services, where such services may often not be central to the organization's chief purpose.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-76)

In 2010, during a debate on the [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act"), Casey was heckled for his handling of the abortion provisions in the bill and for not taking an uncompromising anti-abortion stance. He was the primary sponsor of an amendment to prevent government funds from being used for abortion services, but when he tried to organize a compromise that appealed to the party's lone Senate holdout, [Ben Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Nelson "Ben Nelson"), he angered some religious groups.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-78)

In 2011, Casey voted against defunding [Planned Parenthood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_Parenthood "Planned Parenthood") and cutting funding for contraception, and for cloture for the nomination of [Goodwin Liu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodwin_Liu "Goodwin Liu"), earning him a 100% rating from NARAL.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-79) The same year, Casey said he supported over-the-counter sale of the morning-after pill for [emergency contraception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_contraception "Emergency contraception").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-80) In the 2012 election, [NARAL Pro-Choice America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NARAL_Pro-Choice_America "NARAL Pro-Choice America")'s election guide endorsed Casey.

In 2015 and 2018, Casey joined two other Democratic senators, [Joe Manchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Manchin "Joe Manchin") and [Joe Donnelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Donnelly "Joe Donnelly"), in voting for bills that would ban abortion after 20 weeks of pregnancy.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-81)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-82) In 2017, he voted for legislation that would have overturned the [Mexico City Policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City_Policy "Mexico City Policy"), which prohibits foreign aid for organizations that provide or promote abortion.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-nationalreview.com-84) His vote prompted anti-abortion activists to question his commitment to their cause.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-nationalreview.com-84) The [National Right to Life Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Right_to_Life_Committee "National Right to Life Committee") criticized Casey for his 2017 vote against the confirmation of [Neil Gorsuch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Gorsuch "Neil Gorsuch") to the Supreme Court of the United States.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-85)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Politico2-71)

In 2018, _Politico_ wrote:

> After a decade in the Senate, Casey has become an increasingly reliable vote in support of abortion rights—scoring as high as 100 percent on [NARAL Pro-Choice America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NARAL "NARAL")'s vote tally in 2016 and 2017 ... although his 2018 rating is sure to be lower.

_Politico_ acknowledged that scorecards "are an imperfect calculation of a lawmaker's position", adding that Casey asserted that he had voted anti-abortion on 13 of the 15 abortion-related measures during his career.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Politico2-71) According to _Politico_, "Like conservative anti-abortion groups, [Casey] opposes the _Roe_ decision and opposes the taxpayer funding of the [abortion] procedure. But like progressive abortion rights organizations, he supports Obamacare, access to contraception through programs such as Title X and funding for Planned Parenthood."[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Politico2-71) Casey considers contraception a tool to reduce the demand for abortions. He has called on greater funding for access to contraceptives, specifically supporting Planned Parenthood's efforts to make them more accessible.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Politico2-71)

In 2022, Casey fully reversed his [anti-abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-abortion "Anti-abortion") position and said he supported legislation to codify national abortion rights.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-86)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-88) He and 45 other senators voted to allow debate to continue on the [Women's Health Protection Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Health_Protection_Act "Women's Health Protection Act") in a roll-call vote on February 28.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-89) He voted for the measure again on May 11 in the wake of the leak of the _[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobbs\_v.\_Jackson\_Women's\_Health\_Organization "Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization")_ decision. He said that if the bill passed [cloture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloture "Cloture"), he would still vote for it.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-90)

### Immigration laws

[Video 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9c/Senator_Bob_Casey_Discusses_the_Border_and_Fentanyl.webm?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

Casey pushes for the [Fend Off Fentanyl bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FEND_Off_Fentanyl_Act "FEND Off Fentanyl Act") to help secure the border after the Republicans block the 2024 [Bipartisan Border bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipartisan_Border_Bill "Bipartisan Border Bill")

Casey supported the Secure Borders, Economic Opportunity and Immigration Reform Act of 2007 (S. 1348), a bill voted down in the [110th United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/110th_United_States_Congress "110th United States Congress"), which would have provided a path to legal citizenship for [undocumented persons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alien_(law) "Alien (law)") living in the U.S. He also supported the Clinton amendment, the Menendez amendment, and the Alaska amendments.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-92) During his 2006 Senate race, he expressed support for the [Comprehensive Immigration Reform Act of 2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_Immigration_Reform_Act_of_2006 "Comprehensive Immigration Reform Act of 2006").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-93) Casey voted to continue federal funds for declared "sanctuary cities".[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-94)

Casey took part in a [Philadelphia International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_International_Airport "Philadelphia International Airport") protest against President Trump's January [2017 travel ban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_13769 "Executive Order 13769").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-Owens_Cassie-30) Leaving a black-tie event to join the protest, he tweeted: "I won't stand by as the promise of America is diminished."[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-95) In May, Casey, nine other senators, and 13 U.S. representatives requested in a letter to the [Homeland Security Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeland_Security_Secretary "Homeland Security Secretary") that they stop the detention of four children and their mothers at the [Berks County Residential Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._Don_Hutto_Residential_Center "T. Don Hutto Residential Center"). Many of the families had been detained there without legal recourse for more than a year and a half. Casey also personally took to social media with impassioned appeals to the White House on behalf of a Honduran 5-year-old and his 25-year-old mother being held at the facility who were facing deportation. They had fled violence and death threats and sought asylum in the U.S. in 2015, but failed their [credible fear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credible_fear "Credible fear") interview. Attorneys had been appealing their case, and the legal team was in the middle of the process of applying for [Special Immigrant Juvenile Status](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Immigrant_Juvenile_Status "Special Immigrant Juvenile Status") for the child when they were awakened at 3:30AM on May 3 by [Immigration and Customs Enforcement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration_and_Customs_Enforcement "Immigration and Customs Enforcement") and put on a plane to Honduras. "This child and his mother deserved better from this Administration. They got the absolute worst", Casey said.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-96)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-97)

In 2019, Casey and six other Democratic senators led by [Brian Schatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Schatz "Brian Schatz") sent letters to the Government Accountability Office and the suspension and debarment official and inspector general at the Department of Health and Human Services citing recent reports that showed "significant evidence that some federal contractors and grantees have not provided adequate accommodations for children in line with legal and contractual requirements" and urging officials to determine whether federal contractors and grantees were in violation of contractual obligations or federal regulations and should thus face financial consequences.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-98)

### LGBT rights

Casey voted for the [Don't Ask, Don't Tell Repeal Act of 2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Ask,_Don't_Tell_Repeal_Act_of_2010 "Don't Ask, Don't Tell Repeal Act of 2010").[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-106)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-107) A longtime supporter of civil unions, Casey stated his support for same-sex marriage in 2013.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-108)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-109) He also supports the adoption of children by same-sex couples.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-autogenerated1-43)

Casey was one of 18 senators to sign a letter in 2019 to [United States Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State")[Mike Pompeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pompeo "Mike Pompeo") requesting an explanation of a State Department decision not to issue an official statement that year commemorating [Pride Month](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay_pride#LGBT_Pride_Month "Gay pride") or issue the annual cable outlining activities for embassies commemorating Pride Month. They also asked why the LGBTI special envoy position had remained vacant and wrote, "preventing the official flying of rainbow flags and limiting public messages celebrating Pride Month signals to the international community that the United States is abandoning the advancement of LGBTI rights as a foreign policy priority."[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-110)

Casey and his wife, Terese, were married in 1985, and have four children.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-111)

In 2023, Casey was treated for [prostate cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prostate_cancer "Prostate cancer").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-112)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-113)

His brother Patrick Casey is a [lobbyist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lobbying_in_the_United_States "Lobbying in the United States") who has reported lobbying the U.S. Senate on a number of issues.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-114)

Casey is Catholic.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-115)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-116)

In 2025, Casey joined the [University of Scranton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Scranton "University of Scranton") as a public service advisor.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Casey_Jr.#cite_note-117)
